entries.title: Trump Stumps for Alaska Republicans and Hands Out Two Pardons
entries.summary: The president handed out the pardons on stage to two mechanics who pleaded guilty to violating environmental laws.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump pardoned two mechanics on stage Tuesday in Alaska, clearing them of their guilty pleas to violating environmental laws.

Stumping for Republicans in Wasilla, Alaska, Trump announced the pardons of Zachary Czubak and Patrick Fleming, a pair of Alaskan mechanics who had pleaded guilty to violating the Clean Air Act. Trump described the pardons as “unconditional.”

“That means you’re as clean as a newborn baby’s ass,” Trump told the crowd, later adding that the pardons were “worth the eight hours in a plane.”

After signing and handing Fleming his pardon on stage, Trump told the pair to say something to the crowd. Czubak called for the reelection of the state’s congressional Republicans, who had lobbied Trump for the pardons. Fleming thanked the president for his freedom.

“This means the world to me,” Fleming said. “It really did destroy us.”

“We’re not criminals,” he added. “We’re not trying to hurt anybody. We want to help Alaskans.”

Trump also referenced Mackenzie Spurlock, another Alaskan mechanic who pleaded guilty to the same violation; the president pardoned Spurlock earlier this year.

Trump made the rare campaign stop in Alaska as the Republican Party makes its final push toward the midterms and politicians in the state hope for a boost in tough races.

Incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan has lagged behind Democratic challenger Mary Peltola in recent polls, while The Cook Political Report changed its outlook on Tuesday for the governor’s race in favor of Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, is the only Democrat in the four-person race for governor. With three Republican candidates, there’s potential for support to splinter between them and hand the race to Kreiss-Tomkins.

entries.title: Jon Ossoff Pledges to Serve a Full Term if He’s Reelected
entries.summary: The Democratic senator said he has “zero interest” in running for president as buzz about a potential 2028 campaign grows.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia pledged on Tuesday that he would serve a full Senate term if he’s reelected next month.

It’s a striking commitment given that Ossoff, who is running in a battleground state, has been floated as a 2028 presidential candidate and has proven himself to be a messaging leader for the Democratic Party.

His promise was made in a debate against Rep. Mike Collins, Ossoff’s Republican opponent in the Senate race, where he was asked almost immediately if he would stay in the Senate if reelected.

“Yes I will,” Ossoff, whose upcoming Senate term would run through the start of 2033 if reelected, replied. “I have zero interest in running for president. I'm not running for president. I'm running for reelection to the Senate.”

Ossoff has previously said he’s uninterested in seeking the presidency, but Tuesday’s pledge ruling it out was the most unequivocal statement he’s made in response to the question.

The candidates argued over affordability, health care, abortion and gun rights at the debate, which was their second time facing off.

Like last week, Ossoff used the stage to highlight Collins and his family and staffers’ ties to far-right views. The debate devolved as the two talked over each other.

Ossoff asked Collins if he would “stop the production of neo-Nazi propaganda from [his] home,” while Collins blamed Ossoff for death threats he’s received and sought to tie him to Hasan Piker, the far-left streamer whose comments about Israel have become campaign fodder.

Ossoff also hammered Collins over a pending ethics investigation into his office’s use of taxpayer funds, which Collins called a “nothing burger.”

While some Republicans in battleground states have distanced themselves from President Donald Trump by opposing certain policies, Collins has defended the Trump administration across both debates, with little exception.

Though Collins appeared to create a little daylight with the president when he was asked about federal intervention in elections, saying that “voting should always be a state's right,” he followed up by pitching the SAVE Act. The legislation, one of Trump’s top legislative priorities for months, would restrict voting access.

Ossoff has consistently led in the polls and enjoyed a huge fundraising advantage over Collins.

National Democrats, confident in Ossoff, appear to believe he’s on track for reelection: On Tuesday, the Chuck Schumer-aligned Senate Majority PAC said it was removing ad spending it had dedicated to Georgia.

Editor’s Note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

entries.title: Judge Extends Order Blocking Trump From Banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico
entries.summary: The judge said the news outlets are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims.
entries.content:
By Hallie Golden and Michael Kunzelman

A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking the Trump administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, as the extraordinary case pitting the president against the media makes its way through the legal system.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed on their constitutional free speech and due process claims.

“Still,” he added, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”

Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Republican President Donald Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order due to expire on Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo while the case is pending

entries.title: Why Obama Is Going to Detroit: El-Sayed Is Facing Skeptical Black Voters
entries.summary: The Michigan Senate race is an “all hands on deck” moment for Democratic surrogates.
entries.content:
GRAND RAPIDS, Mich. — A tense confrontation between a Black voter and Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democratic Senate candidate, over his commitment to a key voting bloc shows the nominee still has some work to do to unite the Democratic base ahead of the November election.

“What makes you different, and how do we know that we trust what you say? Because, historically, the Democrats shit on Black people,” JD Chapman, 46, the head of a youth-mentoring group, asked the progressive Senate candidate last week at a crowded dive bar in Western Michigan.

El-Sayed responded by recounting his family’s story immigrating from Egypt and his experience growing up in Michigan, something he said “doesn't happen without the advocacy and the organizing of Black folks in church communities across the country.” He shared how his education in civil rights history shaped his perspective on systemic oppression and informed his career in public health, crediting civil rights heroes like W.E.B Du Bois, Malcolm X and Martin Luther King Jr. for paving the way for his campaign to become the first Muslim member of the U.S. Senate.

“I owe a deep debt of gratitude to Black folks,” El-Sayed said.

But the professorial-sounding answer didn’t satisfy Chapman, who began walking toward the exit. That prompted Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, the first Black senator from Delaware, who was campaigning with El-Sayed, to step in. Democrats, she said, need to win as many seats as possible in the Senate to enact policies that can help Black Americans.

“We can't do it if we don't have the numbers,” she explained to Chapman. “If we don't do it, hold us accountable. Vote us out.”

El-Sayed Responds to Questions About His Commitment to Black Community 

The pointed exchange illustrates questions El-Sayed continues to face in one of the most hotly contested battlegrounds that could determine control of the Senate next year. Republicans are seeking to portray him as a radical Islamist, launching ugly attacks over his Muslim faith and name. There are doubts among some Jewish Democrats regarding his stance and past comments about Israel, some of which he’s apologized for. And there is lingering skepticism about his candidacy among Black voters, many of whom supported the moderate Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary in August.

“Politicians come and go; they always pandering for our votes at election time, and then they just forget about us once they get elected, especially in West Michigan. I'm sick of that shit,” Chapman, who said he voted for Stevens, told The Washington Sun after the exchange.

He said he may not vote in November, and whether he does will depend on how El-Sayed navigates the cultural differences between Arab and African American voters in Michigan.

“I'll specifically be paying attention to his engagement with the people on the ground in Detroit, where he's from” Chapman said.
El-Sayed Senate Campaign (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)
Progressives view El-Sayed’s candidacy as a blueprint for other insurgent candidates across the country. If he can win in a presidential battleground state like Michigan with a populist message of taking on corporate elites, eliminating money in politics and passing a universal health care program like Medicare for All, others can too. But there are still those in the Democratic establishment who consider El-Sayed, a former public health official who has never held an elective office, a risky bet, one that could result in their party losing a winnable seat in what is expected to be a blue wave election.

Polls show a close race, with El-Sayed narrowly edging out his Republican opponent, former Michigan Rep. Mike Rogers, who also ran for Senate in 2024.

Democratic Surrogates Flood the Zone to Help Unite Base 

Democrats have sought to present a united front despite their divisions. A parade of high-profile names have or are scheduled to campaign on behalf of El-Sayed in the early 2028 presidential nominating state. They include former Vice President Kamala Harris, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy, former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

And later this month, former President Barack Obama will rally with El-Sayed in Detroit, a city that boasts a large African American population. Democrats will need to maximize voter turnout there, as well as younger voters in the state’s college towns, to beat Rogers in November.

“It's all hands on deck,” Whitmer, who backed Stevens in the primary, said last week during her first joint appearance with El-Sayed at a restaurant in Grand Rapids. “We got to get Dr. El-Sayed elected to the U.S. Senate because Michiganders need someone who's got to fight to make our lives better. That's the North Star here.”

Democrats are bullish about the fact that El-Sayed has drawn notably large crowds during his campaign stops in red-leaning areas of Michigan's Upper Peninsula this week, where he’s focused on talking about health care access, the impact of President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada and tribal sovereignty. He’s also picked up the support of some former Rogers supporters who are seeking to put a check on Trump in Washington.

Chris Holman, 77, told The Sun he’s been friends with Rogers for more than 30 years, but he intended to vote for El-Sayed in November.

“I'm looking at it as a vote against Donald Trump,” Holman, an independent and an entrepreneur who owns a business news website in Michigan, said last week as he waited to hear from El-Sayed at a town hall in Lansing. “I feel mostly like the people that Trump allows to be around him are kind of bobbleheads, and that's a very dangerous thing.”
El-Sayed Senate Campaign (4046x3000, AR: 1.35)The only chance Rogers has in the race, Holman said, is to try and tie El-Sayed to “things he's absolutely not tied to, Muslim Brotherhood and all that, and Hamas and all that stuff, and that's just like ridiculous stuff. And I know he knows it, but you know, you got to remember it's about getting elected.”

Republicans have spent millions on ads that seek to tie El-Sayed to past comments made by Hasan Piker, a controversial Twitch streamer who is an El-Sayed supporter, in which he said that “America deserved 9/11.” Rogers also alleged last week in a contentious debate that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, a charge that El-Sayed has denied.

Appearing alongside Rogers at an event in Highland Township, Michigan, on Friday, Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) went even further, alleging that El-Sayed “sleeps in a [Osama] Bin Laden jersey,” a comment that drew a chuckle from Rogers.

El-Sayed shot back with his own insinuation in a post on X: “That’s rich coming from someone who wears his bed sheets out at night.”

The anti-Muslim rhetoric is a particular concern for some Democrats who worry El-Sayed isn’t doing enough to reach out to Hindu voters in Michigan, who make up a small but potentially influential share of the state’s population in a tight race.

“If this ends up close, as close as the primary was, Abdul will regret not engaging Hindu community,” warned Bhavik Lathia, a political strategist from Michigan who served as a battleground mobilization director for Harris’ 2024 presidential campaign. “Because of India-Pakistan tension, the Hindu community is as susceptible or more to Islamophobic messaging coming from the Rogers campaign.”

Rogers Faces Backlash to Trump’s Policies

Rogers, meanwhile, has come under heavy fire from El-Sayed and other Democrats over his support for Trump’s unpopular economic and foreign policies. He has sought to distance himself from the Iran war and Trump’s trade war in Canada, despite his past comments advocating for both. But when asked by a reporter last week about Trump’s tariffs, he continued to defend them, saying they’ve been an “overall positive” for the auto industry in Michigan.
Rogers Senate Campaign (2889x1926, AR: 1.50)Rogers Senate Campaign (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)“If it's good for Michigan, I'll be fighting for it. If it's bad for Michigan, I'll be working with the president and my friends in the Senate to say we've got to change whatever that might be,” he said at a packed barn in Oakland County, where hundreds of supporters donned cowboy hats and rallied for the state’s Republican candidates.

Rogers, who served as chair of the House Intelligence Committee, also told The Sun he disagreed with Trump’s decision over the weekend to import millions of barrels of diesel fuel from Russia. The move was intended to bring down high prices at the gas pump, but one that lawmakers on both sides of the aisle say will only aid Russian President Vladimir Putin’s bloody war in Ukraine.

“You just don't want to give that guy an inch,” Rogers said of Putin.

Still, Rogers can’t break with Trump entirely. He needs the president’s supporters to turn out and vote for him in November. And much of that strategy depends on trying to brand El-Sayed as an extremist and a radical.

But El-Sayed argued that Rogers is the one facing a “base problem” by failing to motivate Trump supporters ahead of November’s elections. Michiganders, he said, care more about bringing down the cost of gas and groceries than his name or his religion.

“My name did not raise your gas prices,” El-Sayed said, eliciting applause at a crowded town hall in Lansing. “My faith is not the reason you can't afford your groceries. My name and my faith are not the reason you can't see a doctor.”

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Oct. 15)
entries.summary: Canadian Americana, British a capella and world music in the woods.
entries.content:
Thursday 


“Out of Bounds” opens at the Kreeger Museum

2401 Foxhall Road NW, 10 a.m to 4 p.m., $15, free for minors

Art, but make it sports? The Kreeger Museum’s fall exhibition, mounted in partnership with Hamiltonian Artists, the U Street gallery and collective, is inspired by athletic pursuits and pushing various mediums to the limit. The exhibit features everything from collage to color field painting, created by both living local artists and icons in the Kreeger’s collection. Through Dec. 31. 

Theatre Week extends

Various DMV theaters, $25 to $65

“By popular demand,” Theatre Washington says it is extending its Theatre Week promotion through Oct. 25. Tickets for “Merrily We Roll Along” at Signature start at $45, for example, and seats at Washington Stage Guild’s seasonally appropriate “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” are $25. Bonus: Several theatres are now allowing patrons to book their Christmas shows at Halloween rates.

More to explore: Comic Riki Lindhome at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company

Friday


Allison Russell at 9:30 Club

815 V St. NW, 10 p.m., $46

What do you call the genre when a Canadian sings Americana music? You call it Allison Russell. The Montreal native — and frequent collaborator with the likes of Aoife O’Donovan, Brandi Carlile and Hozier — comes to 9:30 Club in support of her 2026 album “In the Hour of Chaos.”

Boo at the Zoo

3001 Connecticut Ave. NW, 6 to 8:30 p.m., $35

Break out the costumes early and bring the kids to trick-or-treat where the wild things are. You may have to temper their expectations just a bit, however, since the lions, tigers and panda bears are not giving out candy. Zoo exhibits open for revelers include the Small Mammal House, Reptile Discovery Center and Elephant Community Center. The event also runs Saturday and Sunday.

More to explore: Local rockers Pretty Bitter at Black Cat

Saturday


Tregaron Unplugged

Tregaron Conservancy, 3100 Macomb St. NW, 1 to 3 p.m., free

The 13-acre woodland park in upper Northwest hosts its annual outdoor world music festival, in partnership with Washington Performing Arts. The lineup includes string quartets, jazz, West African dance and drumming, yoga and a sound bath. WPA and Tregaron are also debuting a new GPS-guided “sonic walk” that can be experienced via headphones all year long.

VOCES8 sings “Let’s Fly Away”

George Mason University Center for the Arts, 4373 Mason Pond Drive, Fairfax, 7:30 p.m., $55 to $65, kids through grade 12 half price

Home base for Britain’s premier vocal ensemble is an intimate London decommissioned church, but on tour, the octet’s popularity demands large halls. George Mason’s cavernous hall is maybe not the ideal venue for an octet, but with the Kennedy Center closed, we’ll take outstanding a capella music where we can get it. The repertoire for “Let’s Fly Away” includes everything from renaissance polyphony to Frank Sinatra.

Sunday 


Associates of the American Foreign Service Worldwide Art & Book Fair

Department of State, 320 21 St. NW, 1o a.m. to 3 p.m., free

Many diplomats can’t easily hold yard sales while living overseas. Their inconvenience is D.C.’s gain. Foreign service cast-offs available at this year’s Art & Book Fair include used books, coins, carpets, jewelry, paintings, stamps and textiles. Proceeds help provide scholarships for foreign service workers and other good causes. The book fair also runs Saturday.

“To Hear Her Speak: Black Women and Shakespeare”

Folger Shakespeare Library, 201 East Capitol St. SE, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., free, donations accepted

The Folger’s rotating gallery opens an exhibition exploring the history of Black women and the Bard, from early actors to Toni Morrison. More than 100 artifacts are on display, including costumes, portraits and programs. Other Folger museum spaces, including a printing press demo and dress-up station, are well worth seeing if you haven’t been there since the library expanded in 2024. Through May 2.

More to explore: Chevy Chase Art Walk

entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 3
entries.summary: This week’s group features a goal scorer from Paint Branch and a freshman phenom from Bishop O’Connell.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

With temperatures beginning to drop, it’s starting to feel like playoff soccer weather in the D.C. area. As the postseason inches closer, these six local standouts have stepped up:

Benji Kurtzig, Senior, Forward, Washington International

Kurtzig scored a hat trick in Washington International’s 5-1 win over Spencerville Adventist last week. He netted two penalty kicks and also scored on an impressive free kick from more than 30 yards out. Following the graduation of forward Brown Huffard, who tallied 40 goals and 40 assists en route to first team All-Met and D.C. Gatorade Player of the Year honors last season, Kurtzig has helped fill the offensive void left in Huffard’s absence. The senior is the second-leading goal scorer on his team and leads the Red Devils in assists.

“He’s a tremendously technical player when it comes to his first touch and his body control, whether it be with his head, his chest or his feet,” Washington International coach Andrew Sopher said. “Everyone knows it’s hard to replace a 40-goal scorer, but he’s doing everything in his power offensively to help us score goals.”

Joel Mbi, Senior, Forward, Paint Branch

Mbi was the focal point of a Paint Branch boys’ team that scored a 4-2 win over Maryland 4A heavyweight Churchill last week. The senior striker scored a hat trick in the upset victory, pushing his tally to 19 total goals this season. Under coach David Obeng-Darko, the Panthers have risen from a middling Montgomery County squad to one of the most dangerous teams in the area.

“You see the players look up to [Mbi],” Obeng-Darko said. “If Joel comes into the game and says ‘Hey guys, I’m playing today, follow me,’ everyone will follow him … he carries that much, as the kids would say, aura.’”

Cami McIntosh, Freshman, Forward, Bishop O’Connell

McIntosh has already emerged as a top scoring threat in her first season for the O’Connell girls. The freshman is already up to 17 goals and eight assists on the year, including four goals and an assist last week in a win over Bishop McNamara. She added a penalty kick goal in a draw against fellow WCAC contenders St. John’s.

“She’s a standout every game,” coach Alberto Starace said. “If she’s not scoring, she’s assisting or she’s creating problems for other teams because of her speed, her aggressiveness or just the tactical aspect of the game.”

Noor Neama, Senior, Forward, Churchill

Neama has been on a scoring tear for the Churchill girls, who recently clinched their division title with a win over Walter Johnson. Neama netted the game-sealing goal in that victory, and last week scored hat tricks in lopsided wins over Damascus and Paint Branch. The senior is up to a team-high 13 goals on the season.

“She can read the game really well, and I think that’s what makes her so dangerous,” Churchill coach Haroot Hakopian said. “She understands high-level soccer and sometimes sees things before they develop, which makes her such a dangerous scorer.”

Emma Pryor, Sophomore, Forward/Goalkeeper, Bullis

Pryor is one of several standouts for the Bullis girls, who have their eyes on an Independent School League A division title this season. She led her team to a key overtime win against St. Stephen’s & St. Agnes last week, scoring a penalty kick goal in regular time and providing the game-winning assist in overtime. The do-it-all sophomore also spends time in goal for the Bulldogs.

“[Pryor] always makes a difference, always changes the game,” Bullis coach Dejan Lunova said. “She understands even as a goalie how to move and how to play. … She’s a very important player.”

Javier Vila, Senior, Midfield, Georgetown Prep

Vila has been a consistent offensive threat this season for Georgetown Prep. Last week, the senior scored his team’s lone goal in a 1-1 draw against St. Albans, then exploded for a hat trick in a 4-2 victory over Episcopal. Vila also added an assist in the win.

With wins over St. Albans, Landon and Gonzaga under their belts, the Hoyas look like top contenders in the race for the Interstate Athletic Conference crown.

entries.title: Police Chiefs Are Quietly Signing ICE Deals Without Approval
entries.summary: They are getting funds in exchange for enforcing federal immigration laws — and an earful from locals.
entries.content:
Police chiefs are signing lucrative agreements to deputize cops as deportation agents without approval from elected officials — with some then finding themselves facing a wall of local resistance.

Some small towns put the deals with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on hold. Others have torn up the contracts. And typically mundane municipal meetings have erupted in passionate debate over whether local officers should assist federal immigration enforcement.

"Someone signs, then everyone else says: Wait, what did you just do?” said Alana Greer, an attorney in Florida who runs a group called the Community Justice Project that provides legal support for organizers.

The contracts have brought to city halls the national debate over the Trump administration's aggressive immigration patrols, with some residents expressing fears that the agreements could lead to their neighborhoods being the scenes of the next social media videos of masked agents using force.

The town council in Stinesville, Indiana, got an earful last month when its police chief defended his decision to unilaterally sign a deal that brought in $122,500, enough for three used cars and some body-worn cameras or bulletproof vests. The deal is now in limbo.

Brooklyn Nicole, a chemistry engineer who lives there, spoke up at a town meeting on Sept. 22 and said it was inappropriate that the town was not notified of the deal signed in February.

“That’s the thing I hate the most about it. It comes off as shady and inappropriate,” Nicole said in an interview. “I just don’t think we should be supporting any kind of violence against anybody. For me, it’s a slippery slope. Maybe you’re just transporting people now. But that could escalate."

Signing the ICE contract without telling the town "sets a precedent for getting away with whatever you want," Nicole said. "It’s a reserve police department. They work for us, and they should listen to the public."

The number of partnerships between Immigration and Customs Enforcement and local law enforcement across the country has exploded in President Donald Trump's second term, according to ICE's database. There were 150 contracts in Trump's first term; there are now 2,631 and counting.

The Trump administration plans to spend $1.6 billion on the program through September 2027, a sum that far exceeds previous funding. The money boost comes to the Department of Homeland Security through the 2025 reconciliation law, according to the department.

The Trump administration has advertised $7,500 for equipment per trained officer, $100,000 for new vehicles per partnership, salary and benefits reimbursement and overtime funds. A DHS brochure features a simple equation: “Your Agency + Federal Law Enforcement = SAFER COMMUNITIES.”

In reality, the finances of the program don’t always pan out for the law enforcement agencies. A University of North Carolina study found that the pioneer in that state, Mecklenburg County, spent $5.3 million in the first year of an ICE partnership that it later canceled in 2018, and nearby Alamance County spent $4.7 million during its first year, mostly in immigrant detention costs — until the Obama administration’s Justice Department yanked away the program over a finding of racially discriminatory policing tactics under Sheriff Terry Johnson. (The same sheriff inked a new deal in 2020.)

In the rural borough of Clarion, Pennsylvania, the monthly meeting for October began with a hat-in-hand address from Police Chief William Peck IV over the way he’d signed the deal in July. Elected officials didn’t find out about it until sometime in August. The anger that simmered over the next few weeks manifested at that hearing.

“Oh my gosh, we had 50 to 80 people, which to us is a huge crowd. The council meeting was just filled with outraged people that we had entered this agreement,” Borough Council President Carol Lapinto said in an interview. “Bill said he felt a police car is not worth dividing the community or council. He's such a good-hearted person, and he just felt terrible about it.”

By the night’s end, the deal was kaput.

“We try to be really transparent, and this really shot us down. It just raised questions,” Lapinto said. “You need to check with your councils to discuss it before signing anything, because it ends up being the elected officials' responsibility."

The heartbeat of Clarion is the PennWest University campus, which hosts foreign students studying biology, chemistry or economics who are vulnerable to ICE’s aggressive patrols.

Last month, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported how in Schuylkill County alone, 14 law enforcement agencies have taken on ICE duties — setting up human checkpoints outside a popular ice cream shop called Freeze and inspecting trucks on rural highways — creating what one columnist there called “a climate of fear.”

The ICE partnerships are dubbed 287(g) agreements, in reference to the section of the Immigration and Nationality Act that allows state and local law enforcement agencies to engage in work normally reserved for deportation agents. Nearly three in four agreements are for a "task force" model, in which officers are essentially deputized as ICE agents.

In Pitcairn, a suburb of Pittsburgh, residents discovered that their police chief signed on to the ICE program in July without first getting council approval. Council member Lisa Petrosky on Sept. 14 cautioned about the lack of transparency and her concerns over potential town liability if a local officer gets sued over bad behavior in service of ICE.

Police Chief Scott Farally stood up and got defensive. “Every one of my officers is in agreeance with this program,” he said. “I don’t know where this came to light that I gotta ask the borough for the operation of the police department. I don’t … I can run my department.”

“I think you guys are a little lost on this,” he continued, noting that DHS also works on counterterrorism.

Council member George Burkhardt later expressed his frustration, saying: “I don’t agree with the way it went down. I totally don’t agree with it.”

Another council member, Deborah Marto, emphatically expressed her indignation about illegal immigration but still noted, “I was pissed when I found out. Somebody should have communicated at least with us so we could have done proper protocol.”

However, the council didn’t vote to cancel the deal — marking a tepid approval of something they never had a say in to begin with.

The agreements have also become something of a litmus test at the state level. Texas passed a law in 2025 requiring almost every county with over 100,000 people to sign onto one of these deals, and Florida that same year passed a law that incentivizes localities to join these partnerships.

Meanwhile, 10 Democratic-leaning states have outright banned cooperation with ICE through 287(g) agreements, a list that this year added Maryland and New Mexico. A Virginia law along those lines has been blocked by a federal judge, allowing existing deals to continue for now.

In New York, 15 sheriffs have sued Gov. Kathy Hochul to counter the “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act” law that was passed in May, saying the Democrat has decided “to second-guess the independent judgments of elected sheriffs concerning federal cooperation with immigration enforcement.”

Mateo Forero, an attorney with Federation for American Immigration Reform representing the sheriffs, said 287(g) agreements have “exploded” in popularity but stressed that it isn’t always about the money.

“They did not receive any kind of reimbursements,” he said. “Because for our clients it’s not about getting a bounty. The sheriffs in New York made a policy judgment that cooperating with immigration enforcement serves the public safety in the communities they serve that elected them.”

The fight over the ICE agreement in Stinesville has escalated into a statewide drama itself.

It was riddled with problems from the start. The 287(g) agreement was signed by Shane Pittman, who was merely the deputy police chief at the time. The town council claims it didn’t hear about it until the summer and still hasn’t voted on it — despite a state law that clearly says any Indiana political subdivision “must, by ordinance or resolution, enter into a written agreement.”

Pittman, now the chief of police, made an apology of sorts at last month’s town meeting, saying the department “fell short on procedure.”

“This town is better off when decisions like this are made out in the open,” Pittman said. “Going forward, going forward, my promise to you is simple. We're going to do this the right way. We're going to be transparent, and we're going to keep what's morally and ethically right in the center of every decision that we make.”

But when he invited the public to ask him questions, Pittman raised a caveat: He wouldn’t provide any answers about “specific activity” because the 287(g) agreement forbids a department from sharing information without first running it through ICE. An agreement of dubious legality was being portrayed as already binding.

Last month, the Monroe County Commission, where Stinesville is located, chastised the town and passed a resolution that concluded the deal “was inconsistent with the democratic process, with the letter and spirit of Indiana's open government laws, and with the values of this community.”

Town officials then got particularly annoyed when the county engaged in what was perceived as epic trolling during the annual Stinesville stone quarry festival. Monroe County took part in the parade by sending over a big red snowplow with a sign taped to the side that read, “READY FOR AN ICE STORM.”

Indiana’s Republican attorney general, Todd Rokita, has gotten involved, putting out a curiously timed legal advisory opinion that blessed Stinesville’s ICE deal — issued the morning before town officials met to vote on it and just a week after his office inked its own 287(g) agreement.

“By the way, every county sheriff across the state should be — and can be — doing what we’re doing. And what sheriffs across the nation are doing,” his office said in a statement.

Christie Popp, an immigration lawyer in the nearby state capital of Bloomington, said the attorney general’s sudden rereading of the law “has many errors and contradicts the plain text of the statute.”

Although the attorney general now claims the statute doesn't apply to deals with the federal government, Popp pointed out that it specifically regulates cooperation between law enforcement agencies. And while Rokita has determined police chiefs have the authority to enter these agreements, Popp and others have noted that Pittman wasn’t even the actual chief when he signed the deal.

“We cannot ignore one important statute just to further Rokita's desire to eject all brown foreign nationals from Indiana,” Popp said.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: A Math Problem for D.C. Voters
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 14, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Ranked-choice voting headaches, jury nullification and D.C.’s first dedicated padel facility. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. Temperatures threaten record highs for the date. Fortunately, October warmth doesn't have the sizzle of midsummer heat. Full forecast from Capital Weather.


THE LATEST

Opening your D.C. mail-in ballot this week? If you’re scratching your head over how ranking choices works in an at-large race with two winners, you’re far from alone.

District residents used ranked-choice voting in June’s primary, but The Washington Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports that applying the system to a multiseat race in the general election brings a mathematical twist. To satisfy the Home Rule Charter’s mandate that an at-large seat go to a non-majority party, the District combines the two open seats onto a single ballot grid. Because standard ranked choice rules only allow one active vote per ballot at a time, a top choice winning the first seat locks the ballot, meaning secondary choices for the second at-large seat are never counted.

This new math has shifted campaign strategies for at-large candidates, leading frontrunners like incumbent council member Elissa Silverman and Democratic nominee Oye Owolewa to urge voters to rank them first.

D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson floated an emergency fix over the summer, but pulled the measure following pushback from architects of Initiative 83, the ballot measure that brought ranked-choice voting to the District. Meanwhile, the Board of Elections says its educational mailers are running behind due to contracting red tape, leaving some frustrated residents to decipher the new system as voting gets underway.





DEEP DIVE

James Comer AP - 26161518592412 (3600x2401, AR: 1.50)
House Republicans have launched an investigation into D.C. activists over the practice of “jury nullification,” The Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports.

The investigation is so far targeting two D.C. organizations, Harriet’s Wildest Dreams and Free D.C., which have hosted trainings for potential D.C. jurors. Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky), who chairs the House Oversight Committee, alleges the groups are advocating for the long-debated practice of jury nullification, which happens when a juror opts to acquit someone — even if they think the accused person is technically guilty — because they object to the law or to the decision by prosecutors to charge the person.

Discourse around jury nullification in D.C. took on steam last year after a streak of cases where grand juries declined to indict people who had been arrested for allegedly assaulting federal officers. Perhaps the most high-profile of those cases involved the so-called “sandwich guy,” who became a symbol of D.C.’s anti-Trump resistance after he hurled a sandwich at a federal agent in a self-described act of protest.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Increased demand and unseasonably warm weather has prompted difficult circumstances for PJM Interconnection, the main supplier of electricity for the Washington region and a good portion of the mid-Atlantic. PJM says it is taking steps to ensure that there’s no interruption in electric supply, including putting off planned maintenance work that often takes place during the fall months and working with big users of electricity to decrease their immediate demand. Regulators in D.C. tell The Sun that rolling blackouts are not expected in the region.

A tree better not fall, or else. That was the message from U.S. Judge Ana C. Reyes on Tuesday, when she issued a temporary restraining order barring the Trump administration from cutting down any more trees at East Potomac Park. She also mandated a three-day advance notice on “any irreparable modification to any permanent form or feature of the East Potomac Golf Course." The order follows a scathing hearing Monday where she accused the Trump administration of misleading her on its evolving plans for the golf course.

A group of congressional Democrats is asking the Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Department to stop using an AI tool to assist with D.C.-area flight management, concerned that Congress has not received safety evaluations, testing reports or information about how workers were trained to use the technology, The Sun’s Michelle Del Rey reports.

Padel to the metal: The city’s first dedicated padel facility — Capital City Padel Club — will open this spring at Bridge District in Southeast D.C. The club will feature three outdoor courts and clinics for players of all skill levels.

The D.C. Council is considering more oversight at Saint Elizabeths Hospital, as the Southeast D.C. psychiatric facility continues to face safety and financial issues, The Washington Business Journal reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Virginia voters are casting ballots early in greater numbers than in the last midterms, with less than a month to go before Election Day. According to the Virginia Public Access Project, 531,375 Virginians have voted early as of Oct. 12, nearly double the number who voted by that point in 2022.





FROM MARYLAND

Education leaders in Montgomery County spoke at Tuesday’s County Council meeting in favor of a bill that would establish a $2,500 property tax credit for public school employees who own a home in the county, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

The Montgomery County Board of Education vice president, Brenda Wolff, told council members the board does “everything it can to provide fair and competitive wages, but there is a limit to what is possible on our end,” suggesting the council and board combine their efforts to address increasing inflation. The bill moved to a work session scheduled for Oct. 29.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND


For early trick-or-treaters: Boo at the Zoo, Friday through Sunday.

For global music fans: Tregaron Unplugged at Tregaron Conservancy, Saturday.

For collectors: Worldwide Art & Book Fair at the State Department, Saturday and Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Boone Jenner AP - 26283034264760 (4278x2852, AR: 1.50)
Less than two weeks into a new season, the new-look Caps have offered quite a bit for fans to enjoy. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports that many of Washington’s new additions are playing well and there are times when the team looks like a legitimate contender. But early season games have also exposed some issues, including a lack of depth on defense and a power play that needs work.

Fall sports season continues and The Sun’s Noah Ferguson is keeping tabs on the area’s best high school talent — see his latest selections for All-DMV players of the week in volleyball and soccer.

What to Watch Today

NHL: Capitals vs. Canadiens, 7:30 p.m. (Monumental)

entries.title: Morning Sun: The Matter of Kansas
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The latest from Kansas. A court smacks down the White House press freeze, again. A scoop about ICE body cameras. Obama’s Michigan mission. What yesterday’s Senate debates sounded like. And: Small-town cops vs. their small towns on DHS enforcement deals. 





THE LATEST

Just how real is this Kansas thing? The Sun’s Elena Schneider traveled to the state that is scientifically flatter than a pancake for a story about politics on tilt. “You have a perfect storm brewing,” one Republican strategist told her, “but all of that said, Kansas is red and super partisan.”

So what’s the problem? Take one incumbent Republican senator’s baggage, mix it with one terrible environment for the party, and voila: “They’re going to try and buy it because it’s their best available option,” a Kansas Republican operative said of the national GOP moneybomb currently detonating on state airwaves on behalf of Sen. Roger Marshall. “But it’s not what Marshall is lacking,” the operative went on. “He’s lacking a ground game and a good message.”

Democrats have the opposite issue. Their nominee, Adam Hamilton, has the bio, the message and the campaign skills to make moves. But he’s still got to make them in … Kansas. “He was convinced by Democrats in high places that the two-party system is too locked in,” Stephanie Sharp, a Republican strategist in Kansas who advised Hamilton in the early stages of his campaign — when he was considering running as an independent — told Elena.

We’ll find out how good that advice was in a few weeks. In an interview with The Washington Sun after an event in Lindsborg, Kansas, last week, Hamilton called the GOP spending “a great compliment.” He added: “It means you’re recognizing that there are a lot of Republicans who might be voting for a Democrat in the state of Kansas, and that’s actually what’s happening.”

More: Trump Stumps for Alaska Republicans and Hands Out Two Pardons • Press Groups Compare Gov. Moore’s ‘Censorship’ of Sinclair News Outlets to Trump’s Media Ban • WaPo: U.S. probe of Ilhan Omar focuses on birth date, citizenship papers, people familiar say





FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Breaking overnight: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a preliminary injunction in the CNN, Politico and MS NOW lawsuit against the White House, extending the status quo that it can’t deny reporters from those outlets hard passes while the case proceeds. In a 26-page order, Kelly dismissed the Trump administration’s reliance on national security as a reason to deny access.

“Defendants — for whatever reason — chose not to submit any other material, classified or unclassified, under seal or ex parte, in support of their asserted national security interest,” Kelly wrote. “There is practically nothing national security-related in the record connected to the President’s decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes to which the Court can defer.”

FROM DHS


Scoop: ICE declined bodycam recommendation. The Department of Homeland Security dismissed the suggestion that ICE agents’ body-worn cameras would start recordings if agents drew their weapons or stood near others who turned their cameras on, according to the Government Accountability Office, The Sun’s Jackie Llanos reports. Rather than following the GAO recommendation for automatic bodycam activation, DHS said it will stick with manual activation of agent body cameras during arrests, searches and similar activities.

More: ICE Wants to Use AI to Monitor Detainee Calls and Movements

FROM MICHIGAN


Why Abdul El-Sayed is bringing in Obama: The Sun’s Igor Bobic reports from Grand Rapids, where an AES event to bolster his support among Black voters got awkward as one local advocate, unsatisfied with an answer from El-Sayed, began walking out. Democratic surrogate Lisa Blunt Rochester, the first Black senator from Delaware, had to jump in to try to smooth things over.

FROM THE DEBATE STAGE


All you need to know from last night’s Senate debates: It was sequel night behind the lecterns in Georgia, Iowa and Maine.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Georgia) pledged to serve out a full term if he’s reelected. “I have zero interest in running for president,” he said. Time to cash out those 2028 bets? Maybe, but also he’s been saying that “zero interest” line for a while.

Over in Iowa: “We need to lower gas prices, we need to lower diesel prices, but I don’t think we need to make a deal with Russia to do it,” Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, said, attempting to put more distance between her campaign and Donald Trump. Ironically, the president’s deal on Russian diesel is supposed to help candidates like Hinson with big agricultural electorates after more than a year of tariffs and energy price spikes.

In Maine, they’re still arguing about how important Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ congressional seniority is. “Look, Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Trump’s command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger,” Democratic nominee Troy Jackson said.

Collins suggested earlier in the debate that Jackson will never have her juice. “He has said that the past two governors vetoed 100 of his bills,” she said, referring to his time as a state senator. “He couldn’t work with a Democratic governor nor a Republican governor. If Troy wins, that is the record he’ll bring to Washington.”





ON NOTUS PODCAST

From your favorite podcast app: Sen. Brian Schatz, who is poised to be the second-ranking Democrat in the Senate next year, sat down with The Sun’s Igor Bobic this week to give his frank assessment of the midterms. While Schatz thinks his party will do well, he cautioned against Democrats thinking winning was about them.

Trump “has sort of driven people into our arms, and if people give us a chance, we should understand that we’re sort of the rebound boyfriend,” Schatz said. “They’re going to give us a first date. They’re not trying to marry us. They are just sort of being forced into our arms.” And that means Democrats are going to have to work on a legislative agenda that’s more broadly appealing if they want those voters to stick around in 2028.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Police vs. elected officials on ICE deals: Typically mundane municipal meetings have erupted in passionate debate in some cities across the country after police chiefs have signed enforcement deals with ICE without first telling elected officials. The Sun’s Jose Pagliery has a thorough look at the tension.

The chiefs say they have the power to cut these lucrative deals, but the politicians are blindsided when the public finds out. In Clarion, Pennsylvania, Police Chief William Peck IV backed off an ICE deal after a raucous public meeting. “Bill said he felt a police car is not worth dividing the community or council,” the borough council president told Jose. “He’s such a good-hearted person, and he just felt terrible about it.”

But in the Pittsburgh suburb of Pitcairn, Chief Scott Farally refused to back down. “I don’t know where this came to light that I gotta ask the borough for the operation of the police department,” he said. The council and local residents complained, but in the end the deal went through.

entries.title: Schatz Says Democrats Can’t Just Be Voters’ ‘Rebound Boyfriend’
entries.summary: Brian Schatz, the likely No. 2 Senate Democrat next year, says the party will need to prove its worth to voters with an appealing agenda after Trump has “driven people” to them.
entries.content:
Sen. Brian Schatz cautioned that if Democrats win big in next month’s elections, it would be because of President Donald Trump — and Democrats will need to work hard to come up with an agenda to keep voters on their side.

“What's happening out there in the world is not that we unlocked the proper slogan or messaging technique to make sure that people give us a chance, but rather that Donald Trump himself is our best messenger,” Schatz said on the latest episode of The Washington Sun Cast. Trump “has sort of driven people into our arms, and if people give us a chance, we should understand that we're sort of the rebound boyfriend.”

“They're going to give us a first date. They're not trying to marry us. They are just sort of being forced into our arms,” Schatz said.

Schatz, the likely No. 2 Senate Democrat next year, said Democrats will have to prove that they are worthy of their future support.

“Now we have to essentially close the deal over another couple of years, where people settle into, ‘OK. I'm pissed off at the Republicans, I don't like what I'm going through economically, I don't like all this corruption, I'll give these guys a chance,’” Schatz said. “Then we have to be very judicious, very precise, very humble about what we do with that power.”

Schatz said “job one” in a Democratic-controlled Senate would be exerting leverage to end the war in Iran, followed by restoring cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

“I think people will have voted for divided government, and so we need to recognize that what that means is that we're going to be a check against the excesses of this administration and the excesses of unified control, Republican control of Washington,” Schatz said.

Schatz urged a “planful approach” to things like impeaching Trump or members of his Cabinet, even if there are impeachable offenses to pursue.

“It might be emotionally satisfying for 10 seconds, for instance, to impeach the president a third time and then have him be not convicted in the Senate,” Schatz said. “But I'm not sure what that would get us.”

“I think the question at hand is how do you use that solemn responsibility and power in a way that gives the people what they've been asking for, which is to slow down all this corruption and all this madness,” Schatz said.

Schatz said that a Democratic majority in Congress should instead use the appropriations process to reshape the trajectory of the federal government.

“We already got the legislative text written to constrain the chief executive, and I think if we take power, that's going to be part of the process of getting appropriations done,” Schatz said. “I just think we have to use those powers not to punish anyone in particular but to kind of recalibrate things so that the government itself is stabilized.”

With some Democratic candidates having called for a change in leadership, Schatz said he still expects Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer to pursue another session atop the caucus.

“I’m not his spokesperson,” Schatz said. “I’m trying to be the whip, but I’m not whipping for him, that’s his job,” Schatz said.

Schatz also said he has “no indication” that Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania) is considering changing parties after he recently brushed off a question about being the caucus’ 51st vote. Schatz said he will continue to “double check that everybody's part of the coalition.

The Washington Sun Cast is a weekly podcast where Washington Sun reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.

entries.title: Republicans Are Trying to Spend Their Way Out of Disaster in Kansas
entries.summary: “It’s hard to believe we’re messing around in Kansas,” one Republican strategist said.
entries.content:
HUTCHINSON, Kan. — A retired farmer who voted for Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in 2020 is now backing Adam Hamilton, his Democratic challenger, because the senator’s been a “yes-man” for President Donald Trump. A community college instructor and registered Republican said she’s supporting Hamilton because he’s “a true moderate.”

Ed Berger, an 81-year-old self-described “Republican-leaning” voter who declined to say if he’d voted for Trump before, said it’s the president’s tariffs, the war in Iran and spiraling diesel and gas prices that’s making Kansas competitive.

“What’s happening here, you see it in a lot of races across the country right now,” Berger said.

It’s these frustrated voters — hundreds of whom showed up in central, rural Kansas to hear from Hamilton, some donning “Republicans for Hamilton” pins — who are putting Kansas in play. Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist Church congregation in the country, is tied in public polling with Marshall, a doctor who was first elected in 2020.

The dead heat in this state that hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century “is a microcosm of all of Republicans’ problems nationally,” said a national GOP pollster, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. The race now also epitomizes the Republican strategy to save their Senate majority.

Republicans are pouring money onto the problem. The Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP-aligned leadership PAC, has funneled $14 million to Kansas, cutting from some of its buys in North Carolina, where the Democratic candidate holds a commanding polling lead. Nationally, Republicans spent $200 million more on ads in September than Democrats, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. In Senate races alone, pro-Republican groups have outspent Democrats by nearly $300 million across eight statewide contests, AdImpact found.

“Kansas Republicans have historically relied on significant turnout west of Kansas City, and if that comes, Marshall will be fine, but if that doesn’t materialize, you’re going to have problems,” the pollster said. “That’s why the infusion of cash here should, hopefully — and that’s the important word here, hopefully — do enough to mitigate the biggest problem Republicans face this cycle, which is turnout.”

National Republicans hoped their enormous financial advantage would blunt the toxic political environment. They’re dropping millions on ads attempting to disqualify their Democratic opponents and buoy their deflated base. And while that cash has helped Republicans stay competitive in some states, there’s fires popping up across the map.

“It’s hard to believe we’re messing around in Kansas or South Carolina,” one national Republican strategist lamented, referring to the $5 million the Senate Leadership Fund put into South Carolina to shore up Sen. Darline Graham. In Kansas, “you have a perfect storm brewing,” said a second national GOP strategist, “but all of that said, Kansas is red and super partisan.”

The hope, Republicans privately acknowledge, is to buy their way out of their Kansas problem.

“They’re going to try and buy it because it’s their best available option, but it’s not what Marshall is lacking. He’s lacking a ground game and a good message,” said a Kansas Republican operative, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly. “Marshall’s a bad candidate running a bad campaign in a bad cycle, but he’s got a 10-point cushion to work with. He might use most or all of it, but he still wins.”

Hamilton called the GOP spending onslaught “a great compliment” when asked about it after speaking to more than 150 people at Bethany College in Lindsborg, Kansas, last week — where he led the audience in singing the hymn “All Creatures of Our God and King.” 

“If you are giving us $14 million in Kansas — in Kansas — that means you're afraid,” Hamilton said, “and it means you're recognizing that there are a lot of Republicans who might be voting for a Democrat in the state of Kansas, and that's actually what's happening.”

Democrats are putting up their own answer. Senate Majority PAC, the group closely aligned with Democratic Senate leadership, added $5 million to the race last weekend. People Over Politics, another pro-Hamilton super PAC, added $3 million to its own ad buys earlier this month, bringing it to $6 million in spending.

Kansas has been a trouble spot for Republicans before. But, as one senior Republican strategist put it, “there’s always a Kansas bailout.” A pattern appears to be repeating: This week, Axios reported that Chris Grant, a top Trump campaign operative, would join the Marshall campaign’s efforts in the final weeks.

In 2014, then-Sen. Pat Roberts (R-Kansas) brought in national consultant Corry Bliss to take over his campaign amid concerns about independent Greg Orman’s challenge (Roberts ultimately won by 11 percentage points). In 2020, Marshall led state Sen. Barbara Bollier by just 4 percentage points in public polling in October, but he ultimately prevailed by 11 points.

“Kansas has seen this song and dance over the decades,” said Rob Fillion, the executive director of the Kansas Republican Party. “Now, I’m a realist, and I don’t think Roger Marshall is going to win by 11 points, just because it’s a midterm election — but I see that as the reason he still wins. Republicans typically come home, and I think Republicans are hesitant to take polls.”

Trump is taking another step to bring Republicans home: He plans to host a rally in Wichita next week, extending a run of campaign stops in states that his party won comfortably just two years ago.

In a statement, a Marshall spokesperson said “Kansans have a clear choice” between “a senator who has fought for and delivered major wins for our farmers” and “a Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat.”

Samantha Cantrell, a National Republican Senatorial Committee spokesperson, called Hamilton a “pedophile protector who would vote with Democrats like Chuck Schumer,” referring to local coverage of Hamilton’s handling of a report of child sex abuse at a church camp two decades ago.

But Kansas Republicans said Hamilton’s unique profile, coupled with Marshall’s own weaknesses, puts this seat in particular danger. “People know Hamilton, his church, for years,” said a second Kansas GOP operative, granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly.

“Hamilton has a lot of name recognition and he’s well respected, while Roger Marshall has lost touch. That’s the feeling on the ground,” they added. “Marshall is not charismatic, and he’s had a slew of problems pop up.”

Those problems include reports of him suing more than 700 patients, some of whom were arrested for missed court dates. Marshall has also spent taxpayer money traveling to Sarasota, Florida, where he once owned property, but he told KAKE last week that accusations by the Hamilton campaign that he lives in Florida are “all lies.”

Interest in Hamilton, even in rural Kansas, was on vivid display last week as he swung through standing-room-only stops in Salina, Lindsborg and Hutchinson, a trio of small cities that dot central, rural Kansas and cut through Marshall’s former congressional district. Hamilton laces his stump speeches with biblical passages, integrating call-and-responses from the crowd in his storytelling that demonstrates his years delivering sermons.

“I was watching President Trump's inauguration, and I was praying, ‘God, please give him wisdom. Please help him have compassion.’ … I can tell you, just because you're a pastor does not mean your prayers are answered,” Hamilton said to laughter in the crowd, crammed inside a Salina bookstore.

Hamilton initially considered running as an independent, but ultimately “he was convinced by Democrats in high places that the two-party system is too locked in,” said Stephanie Sharp, a Republican strategist in Kansas who advised Hamilton in the early stages of his campaign. Sharp, a member of Hamilton’s church, said Hamilton knows he must win Republicans and independents because Democrats make up only a quarter of the electorate, and “no one wins with a quarter of the voters.”

He’s leaned into those differences with his party on several issues, including on who might lead the Senate caucus in 2027. He won’t vote for Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, he said in an interview. (“No disrespect to him,” he added.)

“It's time for new leadership, time for younger leadership, time for fresh ideas, and in Kansas, Chuck Schumer is a liability, not an asset,” Hamilton said. “And that's true, I think, almost in every state in the union.”

That pitch, Democrats hope, will mean more coming from a candidate without a voting record and with an in-state brand. He’s also capitalizing on a strategy laid out by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly, a moderate who maximized turnout in the Kansas City and Wichita suburbs and lost by less in the rural counties like those Hamilton campaigned in last week.

Hamilton isn’t positioning himself as the proverbial fighter, like other Democrats this fall. Instead, at Bethany College he called himself a “radical centrist,” not the “milquetoasty middle.” He is “just as determined to try to listen to those liberals” and “just as determined not to demonize the conservatives,” he said.

“He’s able to bring conservatives along on issues like ICE, and he’s able to bring progressives along about abortions. He doesn’t want abortion, but he doesn't want women bleeding out,” Sharp said. “He’s so good at explaining the humanity of an issue, explaining the gray.”

Leaning into his Christian values appealed to James Bowden, a 39-year-old independent who attended a packed meet and greet at the Red Fern Booksellers in Salina. He “dragged” his mother, Nancy, a Trump voter, to hear Hamilton’s pitch because he wanted her to vote with “the knowledge of who they are, rather than the rumor of who they are.”

Nancy Bowden said that while she “agrees with” Hamilton “on a lot of things,” she can’t vote for him because of her “staunch belief about abortion and about transgender.” (“I can’t vote for a Democrat because of that, but I do like him,” she added.)

Hamilton addressed his position on abortion later that day, recounting how his own mother, who was 17 at the time, considered aborting him in utero. Talking to a voter who asked about his position on abortion rights, Hamilton said he felt “this moral tension, and at the same time, a conviction that there needs to be safe and legal access to abortion.”

“I know there are Republicans who are sick of what’s going on right now,” James Bowden said after Hamilton’s stump speech. “I think might dad might be. Mom might have a different opinion.”

entries.title: ICE Won’t Automatically Switch On Body Cameras, Citing Privacy Concerns
entries.summary: Congress’ watchdog urged recordings to start when officers draw their weapons. DHS declined.
entries.content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement will not automatically turn on federal agents’ body cameras, declining a recommendation from Congress’ watchdog.

ICE agents are required to activate their cameras during arrests, searches, brief detentions and other activities. But the Department of Homeland Security told the Government Accountability Office that it wouldn’t implement a mechanism to start recording if an agent draws their weapon or stands near others who have turned on their cameras, according to a GAO report obtained by The Washington Sun before its official release Wednesday.

The stance differs from another DHS agency: U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents’ cameras are set to automatically activate, according to a GAO performance audit.

Carrying out the change for ICE is unnecessary and its risks outweighed the benefits, DHS said in its Aug. 28 response to the watchdog.

“Such triggers could result in the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims, or the recording of bystanders engaged in protected First Amendment activities in areas where camera use is restricted,” the department writes.

An absence of body camera footage from agents’ field stops has come under bipartisan scrutiny following the fatal shootings of immigrants in Houston and Biddeford, Maine, in July and another shooting in Austin in September. ICE agents involved in a shooting last week in New York City were wearing body cameras that were turned on, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during a news conference about the incident.

The GAO insisted in its report that automated cameras would increase transparency, accountability and public trust. CBP and ICE personnel the government watchdog interviewed said they were uncertain of the circumstances that would require them to turn on their cameras.

“This assurance could be particularly beneficial in situations where unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel,” the report states.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Mississippi) called ICE’s rejection of the GAO recommendation unacceptable and said he would be introducing legislation in the coming days to ensure all body cameras are automatically turned on.

“This government report shows that DHS’s body worn camera program is deficient and needs to be revamped if DHS is going to be transparent and accountable,” Thompson, the top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, said in a statement to The Washington Sun. “Worse yet, ICE — which has shown time and again it thinks it is immune to accountability — is unwilling to implement automatic activation for its cameras, increasing the risk of missing critical recordings.”

CBP started issuing body-worn cameras in August 2021, but it took ICE until March 2024 to start doing so. Both deployment efforts paused in 2025 following an executive order from President Donald Trump at the beginning of his second term that rescinded orders from the Biden administration.

All ICE field offices received body camera equipment as of Aug. 5, Jeffrey Bobich, DHS’s executive director of financial management and systems, said in the response to the GAO.

Even when the body cameras are recording, the release of the footage they capture isn’t guaranteed. ICE policy says that the agency may withhold the release of recordings capturing serious bodily injuries or deaths under “specific and compelling circumstances justifying an objection to public release that cannot be resolved by redaction or other means.”

As of September 2025, no ICE agents had received written reprimands for lack of compliance with body camera policies, according to the report. Only one CBP agent had been reprimanded.

entries.title: D.C. Voters Face a New Math Problem Under Ranked-Choice Voting
entries.summary: Applying ranked-choice voting to a two-seat general election for the first time has shifted campaign strategies.
entries.content:
D.C. voters opening their mail-in ballots are encountering a fundamental shift in the at-large council race: the pick-two era is officially over.

District residents used ranked-choice voting for the first time in June’s primary under Initiative 83, the voter-approved ballot measure that overhauled city elections. But applying the system to November’s general election — where two citywide council seats are on the line — is creating fresh confusion as ballots land in mailboxes.

For decades, the at-large ballot carried simple instructions: vote for no more than two candidates. Under the new system, voters face a grid prompting them to rank candidates across columns from first to fifth choice. Yet because each ballot contains only one active vote at a time, a voter’s second choice may never be counted.

The new math has forced candidates to reshape their messaging in the home stretch, with contenders aggressively pleading for first-choice votes. The change has also bred friction among voters accustomed to casting two distinct picks, leaving even politically plugged-in residents puzzling over their ballots.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Rick Reinhard, an 80-year-old Mount Pleasant resident who closely tracks local politics, was among those left scratching his head when his ballot arrived last week.

“There was no indication on the ballot that we get one vote for two seats,” Reinhard said. “You rank people, but there are two seats. How does that work?”

What election officials confirmed to The Washington Sun gets to the heart of the disconnect: Under the city’s new rules, voters no longer cast two distinct votes. Instead, each ballot carries only one active vote at a time. If the voter’s top choice leads the field and wins a seat, that ballot stays locked with that frontrunner — meaning secondary choices marked for the second open seat are never used.

A Charter Quirk Meets Partisan Reality

The mathematical friction stems from a unique structural feature of D.C. governance. Under the 1973 Home Rule Act, Congress mandated that two of the D.C. Council’s four at-large seats be reserved for non-majority party members. To adhere to that law, the District combines a two-seat contest into a single ranked race rather than holding separate elections.

Under D.C.’s vote-counting rules, candidates with the lowest totals are eliminated round by round, transferring their ballots to lower-ranked choices until two candidates remain standing. But those vote transfers only happen for voters whose initial choices get knocked out. If a frontrunner stays in the lead and wins the first seat, those ballots freeze — leaving the second seat to be decided without those voters’ input.

In heavily Democratic D.C., that system creates a unique political headache. The Democratic at-large nominee, Oye Owolewa, is widely expected to draw a dominant share of first-choice votes. Because those ballots stay locked with Owolewa throughout tabulation, Democratic voters who rank him first effectively surrender their say in deciding which candidate wins the second open seat.

This dynamic has shattered traditional campaign playbooks. In previous elections, voters could easily split their two selections between a Democrat and an independent candidate. Now, because a top-choice vote for a frontrunner swallows down-ballot power, candidates are locked into a zero-sum fight for the top spot.

Independent incumbent Elissa Silverman has shifted her strategy to explicitly warn supporters that ranking the Democratic nominee first invalidates their vote for her, urging them instead to “Rank Elissa #1.” Owolewa, meanwhile, is leaning into the city’s deep-blue electorate, encouraging voters to lock in his victory by making him their first choice.

The D.C. Council’s chair, Phil Mendelson, says he saw the coming dilemma over the summer. In a July memo to council members, he explicitly warned that under standard ranked choice rules, “voters may not meaningfully participate in the selection of both At-Large members.”

He further drafted emergency legislation in July that would have established a “multi-pass” system — running a second full count after removing the first winner to ensure every voter had a say on both seats. But Mendelson withdrew the measure before summer recess, citing timing constraints before ballots were finalized and stiff resistance from Initiative 83 architects who insisted the general election proceed under the standard rules approved by voters.

“The people who were behind the initiative said, ‘We intended it this way and don’t want it changed,’” Mendelson told The Sun.

Education Delays 

Compounding voter confusion is a delay in official public outreach. The executive director of the D.C. Board of Elections, Monica Evans, acknowledged to The Sun that official education materials, including mailers and palm cards, are running behind schedule due to bureaucratic red tape tied to the start of the city’s new fiscal year. Evans said the board is launching an emergency outreach push via social media and community events as mail-in ballots arrive and voters start making decisions.

Initiative 83 proponents maintain that District voters are well-equipped to navigate ranked-choice ballots, pointing to June’s primary as proof. In a post-primary Survey USA poll commissioned by the national advocacy group FairVote, 78% of D.C. voters said their ranked-choice ballot was simple to complete, while 71% said they understood the system well. Advocates also point out that even with the option to pick two candidates under the old system, many residents regularly cast a vote for only a single at-large candidate anyway.

However, June’s primary featured standard, single-winner contests across the board. November’s at-large race presents a far trickier multi-seat environment.

Brian Strege, the board chair for Grow Democracy DC who helped lead the Initiative 83 campaign, explained that campaign architects deliberately chose single-vote counting over alternative multi-winner systems — like those in other cities that transfer surplus votes in fractional decimals — to keep the vote counting simple for residents.

“We wanted to keep the ballot straightforward and avoid complex, fractional-vote systems,” Strege said.

For now, District voters will navigate the new grid as designed. As for whether the council will revisit the at-large counting structure after the general election, Mendelson indicated that lawmakers will wait to see how the system functions in practice.

“Let’s see how the election goes,” Mendelson said.
