entries.title: Social Security Recipients Will Get a Cost-of-Living Boost Next Year
entries.summary: Some older adults say the increase isn’t enough.
entries.content:
By Fatima Hussein

The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.

The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.

The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.

The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.

The agency's commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”

Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.

Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year's end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.

The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.

She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans' healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”

Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.

“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.

Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.

Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance," given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.

“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is," he said.

Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.

The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.

While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same "would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.

The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.

The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.

Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.

The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren't able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.

Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

entries.title: Prosecutor Weighs Charges Against an ICE Agent Who Struck a Man With His Car
entries.summary: The Texas prosecutor says the hit appeared to be intentional.
entries.content:
HOUSTON — A Texas prosecutor says a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent appeared to use a vehicle to intentionally strike a man who took off running in Houston and that an investigation opened by his office could result in criminal charges.

Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, needed surgery for a broken leg after being hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man's family.

The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors have also investigated a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.

“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”

Tim Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston, said in a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday that “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Spokespersons for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday.

Parra Hernandez has been in the U.S. for 34 years and was on his way to work when the encounter began, according to Espinosa. Espinosa declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status.

He said he saw two ICE agents in Parra Hernandez's room while visiting him at the hospital.

“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.

Teare said ICE and DHS have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.

In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

entries.title: The Ovechkin Farewell Tour Opens With a Capitals Loss to Carolina
entries.summary: The Hurricanes defeated Washington, 4-2, in the first Caps road game since Ovechkin announced that this season would be his last.
entries.content:
RALEIGH, N.C. — For roughly 30 minutes on Tuesday, the Capitals showed they could apply pressure, dictate play and control the puck against the defending champion Hurricanes. And then came the rest of the game.

An undisciplined run led to a 4-2 loss for the Capitals. This was the beginning of the farewell tour for Alex Ovechkin: It was the first road game for the Washington captain since his announcement that he would retire at the end of the season and his final Capitals game in Raleigh for the regular season. Carolina fans recognized his last time in the building (for now) with a standing ovation early in the game. They left happy after Washington stumbled into a series of penalties and failed to protect an early lead.

“You’ve got to learn to manage those scenarios,” said Capitals coach Spencer Carbery. “And play winning hockey when the game’s on the line and when the temperature of the game gets raised.”

Washington outshot Carolina in the first period, 10-8. That did not last. Carolina outshot Washington for the rest of the game, 27-12.

“They started tilting the ice on us in the latter half of that second period and kind of continued in the third period,” said Capitals defenseman Justin Holl, who scored in his first game as a Capital after being recalled from AHL Hershey on Monday. “We just couldn’t find a way back.”

Consistently playing shorthanded made it harder for the team to find a rhythm. The penalty kill has been a relative strength for the Capitals. (“I think our PK has been solid all year,” said goalie Logan Thompson, who did just about everything he could facing a punishingly high shot volume. “Those guys have been balling out for me.”) But it has its limits. After successfully killing four consecutive penalties, Washington cracked early on its fifth and gave up the game-winning goal.

The Capitals’ penalties included a particularly maddening one by Ryan Leonard, who turned in an otherwise strong performance on Tuesday, including two assists. But he was benched after picking up a slashing penalty in the offensive zone with the game tied in the third period. Washington killed the penalty. Carbery didn't allow Leonard to see the ice again until the final seconds of the night.

“You just cannot take a frustrating penalty and slash a guy twice when the game’s on the line,” Carbery said. “It can’t happen.”

Tuesday also provided the first example of how opposing teams may fete the retiring Ovechkin. During a stoppage in the first period, Carolina displayed his career statistics on the video board. The crowd rose to its feet for an ovation; Hurricanes players tapped their sticks in recognition; Ovechkin dutifully waved. The 41-year-old has never been much for sentimentality, but he won't have much of a choice over the coming weeks and months. Some variation of this routine will repeat over and over as more arenas see him for the final time. Yet few of those cities will hold as many key memories for him as Raleigh.

Ovechkin has plenty of history in the building now known as the Lenovo Center. This is where the NHL held its 2004 entry draft, where a 19-year-old Ovechkin folded his massive frame into a small arena seat next to his parents, waiting for his name to be called first overall and for a new version of his life to start. It’s the arena where he scored for the first time on the road. (Asked if he remembered that particular goal, Ovechkin said no, then suddenly recalled the player who gave him the assist: Andrew Cassels, who spent only a few months playing alongside Ovechkin, and who's been retired from pro hockey for two full decades.) And it was home to dozens of fierce divisional battles. There is no road arena that has seen more Ovechkin goals than the Lenovo Center.

He did not add to that total on Tuesday. Away from the power play, his ice time remained fairly limited, with 10 minutes, 31 seconds on the ice at even strength. As much as the arena tribute and the standing ovation, this is part of the long, slow process of saying goodbye.

“Those days, you can’t go back,” Ovechkin said at morning skate, reflecting on his early appearances in the arena. “But the memories are still there.”

entries.title: Inflation Rose Again Last Month, Complicating Republicans’ Midterms Pitch
entries.summary: The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and other consumer goods.
entries.content:
U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections.

The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, up from 0.4% the previous month.

The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, the same as the previous month.

entries.title: Micah Parsons Says Jayden Daniels ‘Cost Dan Quinn His Job’
entries.summary: The Packers star, who played under Quinn in Dallas, sounded off on Washington’s viral blunder.
entries.content:
Green Bay Packers pass rusher Micah Parsons is putting the blame for the Commanders’ end-of-game blunder Sunday solely on Jayden Daniels.

In Sunday’s tie with the Giants, Daniels took a sack in the final seconds of the game and didn’t stop the clock in time for a field goal attempt. Commanders coach Dan Quinn and Daniels have both claimed responsibility for the gaffe, but Parsons said the blame should only go to the quarterback.

“Jayden Daniels probably cost my man Dan Quinn his job, to be honest with you,” Parsons said on his podcast Tuesday. “And, like, I'm a big Jayden Daniels fan. But the reality is, he probably cost a lot of people their jobs this past weekend."

Quinn was Parsons’ defensive coordinator in Dallas from 2021 to 2023 and the two remain close.

After the game, Daniels said the issue came down to situational awareness.

“We have to know the situation,” he said. “We have to relay that as an offense. It starts with everyone, top down. Ultimately, it's on me.”

But Parsons wasn’t buying it. He said teams spend so much time practicing late-game situations that Daniels should’ve known better, and his experience as a starting quarterback gives him less of an excuse.

“I'm a defensive player, and this shit's programmed to me,” Parsons said. “I even know what to do in those situations. … And mind you, it'd be different if Jayden Daniels was a rookie. This is your third year. You've been to the NFC championship game. You've been in big moments before. This is your job to be prepared to understand the game and understand situations. That's in your job profile.”

Parsons added that Daniels is extension eligible this offseason and his blunder doesn’t help his case to get paid, saying that Daniels’ injury history was already a factor that could impact his extension, but Sunday’s tie also hurts him.

“You're telling me, 'Oh, we're going to want to pay this guy eventually $60 million?'” Parsons said. “This cannot happen.”

The NFL star isn’t the only one who expects Sunday’s tie to ultimately impact Quinn’s job status. “Pardon the Interruption” co-host and former Washington Post columnist Tony Kornheiser said he would have fired Quinn in a column this week if he still had his old gig.

Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin, who is now an analyst for NBC, said, “I threw up in my mouth a little bit at the end of the game.”

And ESPN’s Stephen A. Smith, who is never shy about giving his opinion, said on Monday’s episode of “First Take” that Quinn’s days are numbered.

“Dan Quinn, it was nice knowing you as the head coach for the Washington Commanders,” Smith said. “This will be your last season. You will not be the head coach of the Washington Commanders next season. … I know an imminent dismissal when I see one.”

entries.title: MAHA Adviser Gets a Waiver for Conflicts of Interest
entries.summary: Health officials ruled that Tammy Born Huizenga’s financial conflicts are “not so substantial as to be likely to affect the integrity” of her public service.
entries.content:
A government official helping spearhead Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again initiative has “disqualifying” family financial interests that clash with her work, the Department of Health and Human Services ruled in conflict-of-interest waiver documents obtained by The Washington Sun.

But Dr. Tammy Born Huizenga’s financial conflicts are “not so substantial as to be likely to affect the integrity” of her public service, which she may continue, HHS determined.

The conflicts stem from Huizenga’s husband’s financial holdings — particularly, more than $5 million worth of interest in Oak Investors Group LLC, assets of which include pharmaceutical preparation, surgical and medical instrument manufacturing investments, as well as investments in insurance agencies.

Her husband, Michigan businessman J.C. Huizenga, also has an eight-figure stake in Praxis Group Holdings, which provides Food and Drug Administration-regulated packaging for pharmaceuticals, medical devices and nutritional products, according to the waiver, which is dated Sept. 30.

“I have considered whether this case presents an insurmountable concern about the appearance of impropriety and have concluded it does not,” wrote Roger Klein, director of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, the section of HHS where Huizenga serves as a senior adviser providing “strategic leadership and expert guidance to advance the Secretary’s priorities under the Making America Healthy Again (MAHA) initiative.”

Huizenga is tasked with a range of specific duties involving nutritional guidelines, processed foods, environmental exposure policies, consumer product labeling and wearable health technologies, as well as “research on alternative and integrative health modalities” and “strategic public-private partnerships designed to promote patient engagement and informed lifestyle choices,” the waiver indicates.

Her role also includes providing “strategic counsel” to Klein and maintaining “effective liaison relationships with federal agencies, academic institutions, private-sector organizations and nonprofit entities.”

HHS declined to answer specific questions about Huizenga’s conflict-of-interest waivers.

In a statement to The Sun, HHS spokesperson Emily G. Hilliard said that “all HHS employees, including Dr. Huizenga, are required to comply with applicable federal ethics laws, regulations, and financial disclosure requirements. HHS has established ethics processes to identify and address potential conflicts of interest, including recusals or other appropriate measures when required.”

Patrick Shepherd, spokesperson for the independent Office of Government Ethics, declined to comment, saying that while OGE is committed to transparency and citizen oversight of government,” it “does not respond to questions about specific individuals.”

On her personal website, Huizenga says her “passion lies in empowering individuals to take ownership of their well-being by being mindful of what goes into their bodies and what comes out — and to experience the vitality we all deserve.”

Huizenga praised Kennedy’s HHS leadership in an interview with “The Daily Signal” last year, saying “RFK has made it really clear what his priorities are … I love that. We do need to reset here. We’ve been going down a path where the pharmaceutical companies have controlled the narrative.”

This is not the first conflict-of-interest waiver Huizenga has received this year.

On Jan. 13, HHS Assistant Secretary for Health Brian Christine issued Huizenga — then senior adviser for the Office of Assistant Secretary for Health — a waiver because she could not otherwise “perform any substantive duties related to any of the areas” in which she had a family financial conflict. In addition to her husband’s financial interests, Christine indicated that Huizenga had a media-related financial interest that could pose a conflict.

Morris Pearl, chairman of government watchdog group Patriotic Millionaires, said that if Huizenga or any other government official wants to truly avoid conflicts of interest, they should divest conflicted assets or place them in a qualified blind trust.

“Even the appearance of a conflict of interest damages people’s confidence in the government,” Pearl said.

Kennedy himself has been the subject of conflict-of-interest questions, particularly regarding book advances and gifts he’s received this year.

Earlier this year, The Sun revealed that HHS’s then-General Counsel Mike Stuart was engaging in “continued non-compliance” with a signed ethics agreement by personally trading stocks in companies with large HHS contracts. Soon after, HHS reassigned Stuart.

entries.title: DOJ Gives California Election Officials a Thumb Drive and an Ultimatum
entries.summary: The state was given a 48-hour window to comply with the DOJ’s request to segregate the ballots of voters on a list it provided.
entries.content:
The Justice Department is taking extreme measures to root out what it claims are noncitizen voters less than a month before the midterm elections.

California’s secretary of state received a letter and a password-protected thumb drive on Tuesday from the agency, with a 48-hour countdown to cross-reference a list of names against state voter rolls, according to a letter obtained by The Washington Sun. If California does not comply, the Trump administration signaled that it could seek to block certain ballots from being counted, Reuters first reported.

California, one of at least six states with universal mail-in voting, already began sending out mail-in ballots in early October. The letter from acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber, a Democrat, says the DOJ identified voters it “believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot.” A second, identical letter was sent to Dean Logan, who oversees voting records and the county clerk’s office for Los Angeles County.

The DOJ told The Sun that the letters were sent “to ensure that noncitizens who automatically received ballots per California law do not vote in the upcoming federal election.”

“This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring,” a spokesperson for the department added.

The California secretary of state’s office and the Los Angeles County clerk’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The letter instructs election officials to withhold the ballots of voters on the password-protected list until their citizenship is confirmed. For voters who have already received a ballot, theirs should be “segregated” once it’s returned and not counted until their citizenship is confirmed.

“Usually we would not say that some suspicion of noncitizen voters without any additional verification means that we segregate their ballots,” Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law school professor, told The Sun.

Muller added that segregating ballots is not uncommon, such as setting aside provisional ballots or ballots held up by a court order. But he warned that in this case, a significant number of ballots could be contested in tight elections.

California has been at the center of several fights between state election officials and the Trump administration. The state was a key player in the Supreme Court case that blocked a U.S. Postal Service policy that attempted to change mail-in voting rules.

California was also the recipient of a July letter from the Department of Homeland Security that said the state had as many as 190,832 noncitizens on its voter rolls. A similar letter was sent to Nevada that said the state had nearly 15,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS later rolled that back to 185 noncitizens, all of whom were found to be lawful citizens.

Tuesday’s letter is a significant escalation in the Trump administration’s quest to change how states conduct their elections.

The DOJ added that it “will have no choice but to seek emergency relief” if California does not comply. Although states control their own elections, it’s unclear so far whether California will push back on the DOJ’s request. Tuesday’s letter acknowledged that “states are responsible for voter registration, and the Federal Government is responsible for maintaining immigration records.”

The California attorney general’s office referred The Sun back to the secretary of state.

entries.title: Nancy Mace’s Ex-Fiance Charged With Sex Crimes She Detailed in a House Speech
entries.summary: Two of Patrick Bryant’s business associates were also charged with sex crimes and voyeurism on Wednesday.
entries.content:
By Meg Kinnard and Jeffrey Collins

COLUMBIA, S.C. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace's former fiance and two of his business associates were charged with sex crimes and voyeurism on Wednesday over an episode the South Carolina congresswoman described in detail during a speech last year on the House floor about how crimes against women are not investigated thoroughly.

John Douglas Osborne committed sex acts on a 23-year-old incapacitated and intoxicated woman while Mace's ex-fiance Patrick Bryant and Eric Bernard Bowman watched, according to sworn statements by agents from the State Law Enforcement Division, which brought the charges.

The men talked about who would assault the woman beforehand, took photos and recorded the assault, which was also seen on a security system feed at the home in Sullivan's Island, an affluent suburb of Charleston, state agents said. The woman had fallen into a pool and was passed out on a couch covering herself with a pillow, agents said.

Another woman who happened to be watching the feed saw the assault and took pictures and wrote about it in a journal, police said. Mace and Bryant were not yet engaged at the time of the October 2018 assault.

Osborne, 46, is charged with first-degree assault and battery and two counts of third-degree criminal sexual conduct. Bryant, 53, and Bowman, 46, are each charged with voyeurism.

Along with the voyeurism charge, Bowman was also charged with obstruction of justice after agents said he did a factory reset on a cellphone he knew investigators were seeking in a search warrant, and with publishing the name of a victim of criminal sexual conduct after posting the victim’s name and a video of her on X.

Bryant didn't return a message seeking comment on Wednesday, and attorneys who have been listed as representing Bowman and Osborne in other cases did not immediately return messages.

Mace, a Republican, described the assault at length in a nearly hourlong speech in February 2025 that named the men and described other photos and videos found when she looked at Bryant's cellphone when they were still together.

Mace said she “accidentally uncovered some of the most heinous crimes against women imaginable. We’re talking about rape, non-consensual photos, non-consensual videos of women and underage girls, and the premeditated, calculated exploitation of women and girls in my district.”

At the time, Bryant completely denied the allegations. “I take this matter seriously and will cooperate fully with any necessary legal processes to clear my name,” he told The Associated Press.

The State Law Enforcement Division didn't say if their investigation into any of the men is continuing.

After the arrests, Mace released a statement detailing the 25 bills she says will protect victims of sexual assault, harassment or discrimination, including in retaliatory defamation and libel lawsuits that may result from allegations they bring to light.

The Republican, who is leaving the House this term after losing her bid to be South Carolina governor, introduced a proposal this week to require that anyone who brings such a case and loses must pay attorney fees for the defendant.

“Protecting women and holding predators accountable isn’t a slogan. It’s been one of my top priorities in Congress. For too long, survivors have faced broken systems while predators exploited loopholes and walked free,” Mace said in her statement.

entries.title: Freedom Caucus Chair Freaks Out Over Being Recorded in Public
entries.summary: Andy Harris incorrectly cited a Maryland statute to bar a reporter from recording, declaring, "I actually know the law well."
entries.content:
Republican Rep. Andy Harris demanded that police remove a journalist from a press availability he was holding Tuesday night after a campaign forum with a Democratic challenger in Maryland, erroneously citing the state’s wiretap law.

Harris, who represents Maryland’s only deep-red district and chairs the conservative House Freedom Caucus, told a reporter in the group of assembled press that they “do not have my permission to record” after Harris was asked about the Iran war.

“If you record, we will refer you to the prosecutor,” Harris told the reporter. They were working for Capital News Service, a student-run news organization that is part of the University of Maryland’s Philip Merrill College of Journalism, The Washington Sun has confirmed.

Police did not remove the reporter.

Maryland law requires what's known as two-party consent; all parties to a private conversation generally must give permission before it may be recorded. The Maryland Supreme Court said in 2018 that the state’s law applies when a person has a “reasonable expectation of privacy.”

Harris invoked the statute numerous times in the back-and-forth.

“We are in a two-party state, you are not allowed to,” Harris said. When asked why, he responded: “Because I refuse to give you permission to record.”

Harris’ argument happened in front of a crowd of other media, all recording with phones, cameras or audio devices. When multiple people chimed in to tell Harris that it was a public setting, he said, “Do you know the law?”

Harris, who is a physician, insisted he did.

“Actually, I’m a legislator. Yeah, I actually know the law well,” Harris said. “Get an officer in here. She is violating the law on two-party recording.”

Harris ultimately left the press scrum, saying, “She’s ruining all your chances to get an answer about anything. See y’all.”

Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

The spat came after a candidate forum with Democratic challenger Dan Schwartz in Cambridge, Maryland, on Tuesday. Harris is seeking his ninth term in Congress, while Democrats in the state have moved to draw him a more competitive district in the near future.

This story was updated to add the reporter’s outlet.

entries.title: The BBC Says Trump Backed Out of a Deposition for His Defamation Case
entries.summary: The president sued the British broadcaster in December over its documentary about the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the U.S. Capitol.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump has backed out of a scheduled deposition for his defamation case against the BBC, which is now trying to compel the commander-in-chief to sit for a court-ordered interview.

Trump sued the BBC in December, claiming the network defamed him and violated Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act in a documentary titled “Trump: A Second Chance?,” which was broadcast in the United Kingdom in October 2024. The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida.

The British broadcaster said in court filings this week that it repeatedly tried to contact Trump’s counsel to schedule a deposition, and both parties eventually agreed to hold it this Friday. Trump’s attorneys informed the BBC they’d “begin the process of advising those who are responsible for handling the president’s schedule and security detail,” adding that the location and time would be provided later.

But Trump’s attorneys told the BBC on Sept. 28 that the president would no longer be available because of “other matters of national importance” and said they’d identify a replacement date within a few days.

Trump’s attorneys then said they’d make the president available during the second or third week of January, but did not provide a date.

Lawyers for the BBC decried the cancellation in a court filing this week, reminding the president that he “chose to file this lawsuit and, in doing so, he accepted the obligations of civil litigation.”

In July, Trump identified himself as the only person outside of the BBC and its independent contractors “likely to have any discoverable information that is relevant to the disputed facts in this action,” the filing states.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

Trump’s case centers on the claim that the documentary misled voters by editing his speech.

In the documentary, Trump is heard telling supporters, “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you. And we fight. We fight like hell, and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”

But the president didn’t make those comments in that order, Trump’s attorneys argued.

“This fabricated depiction of President Trump during the Speech was false, deceptive and defamatory,” attorneys wrote.

They further noted the BBC omitted additional remarks, including, “I know that everyone here will soon be marching over to the Capitol building to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard.”

In Trump’s complaint, the president wrote that he brought the action forward for compensatory and punitive damages for the extensive “reputational harm inflicted upon him by the defendants.”

entries.title: Judge Blocks Trump’s Taxpayer-Funded Ads Through the Midterms
entries.summary: The spots had continued to run a day after the judge issued a ruling freezing them on Sunday.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump has to keep his administration’s taxpayer-funded political ads off the air through the midterms, a federal judge ruled Wednesday.

Judge Jennifer Rochon’s decision extends her earlier 14-day pause to Nov. 8, giving the plaintiffs — voting rights watchdog Common Cause — time to seek government records and pursue a longer-term injunction. The judge had frozen a $20 million advertising contract and required the Department of Homeland Security to cancel the ad placements.

The decision follows a dispute over whether the administration complied with Rochon’s original order Sunday evening. Common Cause said advertising data showed 570 airings after the order was issued, including 32 on Monday, more than a week after Trump promised to finance the commercials himself.

The Justice Department apologized Monday, explaining that government counsel forwarded the order to agency lawyers Sunday night, but they did not see the email until the following morning. DHS then notified its advertising contractor. The government said it is now complying with the order.

Rochon will consider permanently barring the government from bankrolling the political ads at a Nov. 4 hearing, the day after Election Day.

entries.title: White House Rushed to Install Chandeliers Ahead of a ‘Birthday’
entries.summary: A small firm received a no-bid contract for nearly $50,000, with government officials citing “unusual and compelling urgency.”
entries.content:
It was early June, and the White House had an “urgent and compelling” job: Four chandeliers needed to be installed in the West Wing.

Why the rush?

“In this particular case, the environment of the 250th anniversary, the birthday, and other events [redacted],” reads a previously unreported contracting document dated June 5. “This must happen over the weekend as these must be in place before the June anniversary events.”

President Donald Trump’s 80th birthday fell the following Sunday — June 14 — the same night as the UFC fight on the White House lawn. Trump spent the weekend of June 6-7 away from the White House, at Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey.

The General Services Administration chose Agile1Tech, a Virginia-based government construction contractor, for the chandelier installation. The company had “recently completed the contract which created the UFC viewing/gaming room," the contracting document states.

“Agile1Tech is familiar with how to brace these chandeliers in a structure that may not support such weight,” the document reads. “Given the urgency and the unique structures in the ceilings of the White House, Agile1Tech is the contractor identified to meet this urgent need.”

“Based on the results of market research, the government determined that a limited number of vendors were available, but none possessed the capability to properly install a complex chandelier in a historic environment,” the document continued.

Trump needed to be talked out of installing a chandelier in the Oval Office last year because of its weak ceiling, according to a book by Republican strategist Scott Jennings.

The White House declined to comment on the record for this story.

All of Agile1Tech’s White House work for the GSA came on a non-compete basis. While the government is usually incentivized to open its contracting work to multiple bidders to keep costs down, the Trump administration has a history of giving some of its largest work orders out as no-bid contracts. This includes the White House ballroom project, the reflecting pool renovation and the subsequent reflecting pool cleanup.

Agile1Tech initially billed the government $22,000 for the chandelier installations.

On Aug. 27, the contract more than doubled, adding $27,600 for an “additional 3 chandeliers." Reporter Michael Scherer of The Atlantic noted in a press pool report the day before that “A van for a ‘Chandelier Restoration’ company passed by the briefing room around 12:30 p.m.”

At the time, the White House was working fast to finish major refurbishment and construction work — painting the North Portico and installing a helipad — before the arrival of Chinese President Xi Jinping in September.

Trump has transformed the White House in even more dramatic ways during the first 20 months of his second presidency by demolishing the East Wing to make room for a massive ballroom, paving over the Rose Garden and furnishing the Oval Office with dozens of gold fixtures.

entries.title: Lawmakers Fume Over Breakdown in U.S. Intelligence Sharing With Ukraine
entries.summary: Bipartisan criticism followed reports of issues with intelligence sharing and Starlink satellite access.
entries.content:
Lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle say they are outraged over reports that the U.S. may have knowingly withheld warnings from Ukraine that could have alerted the country to Russian ballistic missile strikes this week.

They also cited a breakdown in internet access provided to Ukraine by the network of satellites run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, questioning whether the twin issues were part of a concerted effort by the Trump administration to get Ukraine to the negotiating table.

President Donald Trump clashed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, telling reporters Saturday that Ukraine needs “a new president.”

Zelenskyy said Tuesday that his country received “no advance warning from our partners” on Russia’s latest strike on Kyiv, adding that it was the second time this week that the country was not warned about an attack.

Trump denied the reports, telling reporters at the White House on Tuesday, “We are helping them and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end.”

U.S. officials told Ukraine that the system used to detect Russian missile launches failed due to "bad weather," CBS News reported Wednesday.

Since the outbreak of war with Russia in 2022, Ukraine’s military has relied on SpaceX for access to the internet via Starlink satellite technology, which is geared toward civilian and commercial use, as well as military-grade Starshield satellites that support intelligence and defense operations. The technology is provided to Ukraine through contracts with the U.S. Defense Department.

This week, Ukraine began experiencing disruptions to its frontline operations after satellite terminals started experiencing signal failures for drone units operating at certain speeds, The Financial Times reported Wednesday.

As a result, Russian strikes killed up to nine people across Ukraine this week, according to reports, and left at least 600,000 people without power, Zelenskyy said.

Initial reports of a breakdown in intelligence sharing and issues with SpaceX’s satellite systems prompted several U.S. lawmakers to come out in strong support for Ukraine.

“Congress has repeatedly made clear that the United States should provide intelligence support to save lives from Russia’s merciless strikes,” the co-chairs of the bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus wrote in a statement Wednesday. “US allies pay for Ukraine's access to Starlink. Restrictions that put civilians in harm’s way are unconscionable and will not be accepted by Congress.”

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), who has been a vocal proponent for Ukrainian military aid, also slammed the Trump administration over the alleged lack of intelligence sharing.

“The Administration’s decision to reduce intel sharing to Ukraine & access to Starlink equates to aiding the invader & the war criminal who bombs cities,” Bacon wrote Wednesday on X. “Does the Administration think it will get ANY support for the remainder of the 119th Congress? Their agenda is dead unless they change paths.”

Hours after several U.S. lawmakers sounded the alarm, Ukrainian Minister of Defense Mykhailo Fedorov thanked Musk and announced that Starlink speed disruptions had been remedied, but that Starshield’s restrictions remained in place.

“Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h is being restored,” he wrote Wednesday on X. “Removing Starshield’s speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine’s defense.”

Musk blamed Trump for any continued speed disruptions for Starshield systems.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” he wrote Wednesday on X. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

The SpaceX founder also said Starlink usage should be “limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

John Roberts, an American military veteran who serves as a senior adviser to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, told The Washington Sun that the restrictions on Starlink could cause Ukrainian drones to lose their internet connection if they fly faster than 20 meters per second, or about 45 miles per hour, making it harder for them to intercept Russian attack drones.

“It’s extremely dangerous,” Roberts said. “We are very dependent on Starlink.”

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) specifically called out Musk for the reported disruptions and questioned whether SpaceX “is doing everything it can to fix a temporary glitch.”

“I'm confident this does not reflect a change in SpaceX policy because if so, intentionally degrading Ukraine's ability to defend itself might be construed as aiding and abetting a mass murderer,” Tillis wrote Wednesday on X. “Can you confirm that's not SpaceX’s intent?”

The Pentagon, SpaceX and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Trump recently clashed with Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s continued strikes on Russian oil refineries, a move that Trump said only exacerbates rising fuel prices for U.S. consumers. Zelenskyy pushed back Sunday in an interview with ABC, saying Trump and others are blaming Ukraine because it’s “more simple” but “everybody in the world understands because of the war in the Middle East, the prices are rising.”

Ukraine and Russia have traded strikes this week despite Trump declaring Sunday on Truth Social that the two countries had reached an “energy ceasefire” — a truce Zelenskyy said he did not know about until Trump’s announcement.

Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan in an interview Wednesday that he felt “betrayed” by Trump’s announcement of the energy ceasefire. He also said it was a “pity” that Ukraine is losing America as a “strong partner” and attributed the relationship breakdown to U.S. actions.

“It's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” Zelenskyy said. “But we are OK that he’s in the middle. But if you are in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side.”

entries.title: ‘Democrats for Mike Rogers’ Super PAC Changes Its Name After FEC Demand
entries.summary: The group has been railing against Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a seven-figure ad campaign.
entries.content:
“Democrats for Mike Rogers,” which is supporting the Republican nominee in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, will no longer officially call itself that in political ads.

That’s because the super PAC filed paperwork to change its name after a demand from the Federal Election Commission.

Citing federal rules, the FEC wrote on Sept. 8 that Democrats for Mike Rogers had to change its name if it wasn’t directly affiliated with the Republican candidate, which it is not.

Karen Whitsett, an outgoing Michigan state representative and the committee’s treasurer, told the FEC on Tuesday that it is complying with the agency’s request and that the PAC’s name is now “TFM,” later indicating that it stands for “Together for Michigan.”

The organization first changed its name to “Together for Michigan” on Sept. 15 before switching to the acronym early last week.

“We trust that this resolves the matter,” wrote Whitsett, who announced her departure from the Democratic Party earlier this year.

Whitsett, who did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment, has repeatedly clashed with Democrats in the Michigan House of Representatives.

The pro-Rogers PAC is already hitting the airwaves with its new name, spending more than $4.3 million since Oct. 6 to boost Rogers’ campaign, according to FEC records.

Having only been formed in August, the PAC has not yet disclosed its donors, although it’s slated to do so later this month.

Democrats for Mike Rogers’ name has been valuable for the Republican’s campaign, with officials affiliated with the group publicly attacking Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed over perceived shortcomings with Black and Jewish Michiganders.
Abdul.El.Sayed.1 (1608x1149, AR: 1.40)“Democrat voters who feel their nominee doesn’t represent them in their values — all hope is not lost,” Rogers said at an August press conference with the super PAC. “I'm not asking you to be a Republican. I'm asking you for the opportunity to earn your trust.”

A recent Marist poll of registered voters found El-Sayed led Rogers by 7 percentage points. The Cook Political Report has graded the race a “toss up,” while Inside Elections rates it “tilt Democratic.”

In recent years, numerous other political committees have been tripped up by federal naming rules.

Among them: Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC, Let’s Fire TRUMP, Ready for Hillary PAC and Stop Pelosi PAC.

entries.title: Reflecting Pool Liner Installation Caused Problems in 85 Places, Inspection Finds
entries.summary: The Washington Post obtained the report, which was commissioned by the company that installed the liner.
entries.content:
Errors made during the installation of the coating on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool caused at least 85 failures, according to a report commissioned by the contractor.

A report from Atlantic Coating Inspection found the “American flag blue” liner crumbled at eight of the pool's 10 joints that divide the concrete slabs of the basin, blistered in nearly 40 places from moisture and chemical fumes stuck under the lining, and peeled away from the basin in nearly two dozen spots, according to The Washington Post, which obtained the report.

Atlantic Coating Inspection referred questions to Atlantic Industrial Coating, the company that installed the coating and commissioned the report, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

President Donald Trump facilitated the renovation of the reflecting pool, which has long had issues with algae and leaks, ahead of celebrations for the nation’s 250th birthday. Trump originally said the renovation would take a few weeks and cost $1.5 million. After two months of work that ended up costing $14 million, the pool filled with algae and the coating cracked.

Trump has attributed the damage to vandals, and the administration charged four people in connection to damage to the pool. Those charges have since been dropped. The Atlantic Coating Inspection report completed on Aug. 6 doesn’t mention vandalism and blames the cracks in the coating on the use of improper materials and the installation’s quick timeline, according to the Post.

An Aug. 14 report from Atlantic Industrial Coating blamed its own work and a flawed repair plan for the issues with the blue liner, not bad actors, according to the The New York Times. 

In a Wednesday statement to The Washington Sun, the Interior Department maintained Trump administration claims that vandals caused the damage to the pool and blamed previous presidential administrations for poor maintenance of the site.

“The Reflecting Pool will soon be opened in a condition better than ever before in its 100+ year history,” the agency said, noting the pool’s water valves, pipes and filtration system were replaced and a new liner had been installed.

The Reflecting Pool was last renovated in 2012 under a two-year, $34 million project aimed at clearing the water and installing a more sophisticated filtration system. Trump announced his renovation in April, declaring the “filthy” water his next beautification project in D.C. He wanted the work to be finished before July 4, giving the contractor just three months from the initial announcement for the project to be completed.

Atlantic Industrial Coating had never held a government contract before but had performed work on swimming pools at Trump’s golf course in Sterling, Virginia. After the initial installation failed, the same company was tasked with repairing the Reflecting Pool.

The Interior Department said Atlantic Industrial Coating was contractually obligated to fix the pool, and it would have been a waste of money to bring in a new contractor. The National Park Service refilled the pool over the weekend.

entries.title: Ticket Resale Platforms Sue D.C. to Block Price Cap
entries.summary: A D.C. law going into effect in January will cap resale tickets at 10% more than their original value.
entries.content:
A group of ticket resale platforms sued D.C. on Wednesday to prevent a law that will cap the sale price of secondhand tickets from going into effect in January.

The D.C. Council passed the Restricting Egregious Scalping Against Live Entertainment (RESALE) Amendment Act in July, capping the price of resold tickets at 10% more than their original value. Ticket Policy Forum, alongside ticketing companies including SeatGeek and Vivid Seats, filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C., arguing the law would upend the secondhand market by significantly restricting the costs companies are able to recover in facilitating resale transactions.

The lawsuit alleged the RESALE Act violates the companies’ First Amendment rights by requiring them to publish the original price of tickets listed for resale on their sites. The filing said there is “no evidence that displaying the original price helps buyers understand what they are purchasing,” and that the council “never considered alternatives that would burden less speech.”

The complaint also said the council is overstepping its jurisdiction by attempting to regulate commerce outside of the District. About 85% to 90% of the resellers’ transactions for non-sports D.C. events in the last year were between sellers and buyers both located outside the District, the lawsuit says.

Secondhand marketplaces let customers buy tickets quickly and easily, “but those benefits are lost when governments impose price controls that do not reflect true costs and economic realities,” the lawsuit said. “Such arbitrary price caps inevitably lead to less competition, less choice, less supply, and more black-market activity.”

Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who introduced the legislation, told The Washington Sun he isn't surprised by the lawsuit and that resale companies have run a “scam” for years, scooping up as many tickets as possible to resell at inflated prices. The law will let fans “finally catch a break on the outrageous price mark-ups,” he said.

The law gained support of local arts venues such as 9:30 Club and The Anthem, with proponents arguing that resellers on secondhand marketplace websites have hurt independent venues.

Audrey Fix Schaefer, the communications director for I.M.P., which owns D.C. venues including the 9:30 Club and The Anthem, said the lawsuit is a “desperate attempt” by ticket resale companies to continue to “gouge and siphon" money out of the District by subverting consumer protection laws.

Fix Schaefer said local venues are tired of seeing their customers abused by “parasitic ticket scalpers” selling tickets for far above face value.

Arts venues aren’t the only businesses affected by high prices, she said. If customers can’t afford to see a show, that means fewer people are spending money at nearby establishments before and after the event.

Critics argue the law gives too much power to the primary ticket markets and could drive the resale market underground, making it less regulated.

The law would require the resale websites to sell tickets at a loss for the companies — or blacklist D.C. events, the Ticket Policy Forum said in a statement. It could also push ticket sales to less-regulated avenues, such as on-the-street sellers or social media, increasing the risk of fraud, the statement said.

“Fans need to know this law won’t deliver the relief it promises,” Brian Berry, the executive director of the Ticket Policy Forum, told The Sun. “It was backed by Ticketmaster, and it exempts Ticketmaster’s own dynamic pricing at concert venues, so prices will keep climbing. Worse, by pushing legitimate sellers off regulated marketplaces, it sends fans toward social media, where scams thrive.”

In April, Ticketmaster’s parent company was ordered to pay nearly $10 million to D.C. residents for “deceptive ticketing practices.”

The D.C. attorney general’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This story has been updated to include statements from D.C. Council member Charles Allen and representatives for I.M.P. and the Ticket Policy Forum.

entries.title: Trump’s New Press Secretary Faces Bar Complaint in California
entries.summary: Katie Zacharia has called herself an attorney in recent television and podcast appearances, but it’s unclear if she’s licensed to practice law.
entries.content:
A watchdog group filed a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday asking authorities to investigate whether White House press secretary Katie Zacharia practiced law without a license.

The Campaign for Accountability lodged the complaint on Wednesday following a report from Popular Information, which said Zacharia, a California resident, has never been admitted to practice law in any U.S. state or the District of Columbia.

Per the complaint, state bar directories typically retain records of inactive, suspended and disbarred attorneys. Zacharia’s absence from the databases suggests she was never admitted at all, the watchdog alleges.

“If that reporting is accurate, Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime.”

Misrepresenting oneself as an attorney in California is a misdemeanor punishable by up to one year in a county jail or a fine of up to $1,000, per the complaint.

Zacharia has presented herself as an attorney at least four times this year through television and podcast appearances, the complaint states.

“Each of these representations conveys to an ordinary listener that Ms. Zacharia is a licensed attorney entitled to practice law,” the complaint states.

While standing outside the White House with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, Zacharia appeared to tell a reporter, “When I moved to China,” when asked where she passed the bar exam.

The Washington Sun has emailed the White House for comment.

Zacharia’s LinkedIn page also offers clues as to where she may have practiced law.

Between January 2024 and March 2025, the profile states, she was general counsel to Fix California, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting conservative policies statewide.

Prior to that, she was an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013, the page states. China does not permit foreign nationals to take its national bar examination or practice Chinese law.

Zacharia hasn’t held a full-time legal position since, her profile states. She graduated from Pepperdine University Law School in 2011.

A law degree does not alone qualify someone to practice law. In California, law school graduates generally must pass the state bar exam and meet other requirements to be admitted to practice.

The Campaign for Accountability is asking the State Bar of California to investigate whether Zacharia violated sections 6125 and 6126 of the California Business and Professions Code.

“Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the organization’s executive director, said in a written statement.

“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime. The State Bar should investigate whether Ms. Zacharia has misled the public about her credentials and hold her accountable if she has.”

entries.title: Hegseth Vows a ‘Hell or High Water’ Push for $350 Billion Defense Boost
entries.summary: The Pentagon chief previewed a post-midterms lobbying effort to break the Republican logjam on reconciliation.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that the Pentagon would aggressively push for at least $350 billion in additional military spending when Congress returns after the midterm elections, warning the money is critical to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul the armed forces.

The remarks preview a renewed lobbying effort for a defense package that remains stalled amid Republican divisions over how to pay for it. The proposal would fund Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense shield, expanded munitions production and $50 billion for drones, which Hegseth called the Pentagon’s “No. 1 priority.”

“We’re in lockstep with the White House,” Hegseth said. “Regardless of what happens in the midterms, we’re running fast — immediately — with the committees, to ensure that that reconciliation bill, at a minimum of $350 [billion], potentially more, ultimately fills up what this department needs.”

Hegseth said Trump’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon spending request remained the administration’s goal, “come hell or high water.”

Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget for fiscal year 2027 would rely on roughly $1.15 trillion in regular appropriations and another $350 billion through a reconciliation bill that could pass the Senate with only Republican support. The administration has separately requested an additional $67 billion to cover costs associated with the Iran war.

The administration faces a narrow window to advance the legislation during Congress’s lame-duck session, particularly if Democrats win control of the House in November’s elections.

Hegseth appeared alongside civilian leaders of the military services at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference. The panel discussion on autonomous warfare marked an unusual gathering that Pentagon officials billed as a show of unity behind the administration’s plans to modernize the armed forces.

Hegseth has launched a succession of initiatives aimed at ramping up the development of autonomous weapons that include a Drone Dominance program and recently announced plans to establish a four-star Autonomous Warfare Command by October 2027, an initiative that would need congressional approval.

The Pentagon has been pushing to put prototype weapons directly into troops’ hands for testing and quick improvement, borrowing lessons from the Ukrainian military’s ability to adapt drones on the battlefield. But Hegseth cautioned that the U.S. could not simply adopt Ukrainian technology because of concerns about Chinese-made parts.

"You can't use everything that's in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it,” Hegseth said. “You've got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned, which the Army's done very well, and then push it through.”

Hegseth compared the scale of the Pentagon’s effort to the industrial mobilization of World War II, arguing the U.S. needs to rebuild its ability to make weapons quickly and in large numbers. He described it as “a generational leap ahead in technologies that nobody else on planet Earth can do.”

“That’s the urgency of this moment,” he said. “That’s what the president expects.”

The panel was interrupted six times by protesters shouting about the Iran war and civilian casualties in the Middle East before security guards removed them.

The Iran war’s unpopularity is just one of the headwinds confronting Hegseth, who’s faced criticism of his leadership and a bipartisan impeachment push in the House. A Democratic-controlled House next year could subject the defense secretary to more aggressive oversight and investigations and block parts of his agenda.

Hegseth closed with a pitch to the large gathering, warning that the Pentagon’s ambitious plans — including Pentagon deals to expand munitions production — hinge on lawmakers approving the additional money. Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg has led efforts to negotiate agreements with Lockheed Martin, RTX and other big defense firms to beef up weapons production.

“The deals the deputy is cutting, the drones that this will require, all of those investments are part of reconciliation, of that $350 [billion],” Hegseth said. “And if you’re a part of talking to the people who are making those decisions, the coming months will be critical.”

Rebuilding the U.S. military “to meet the threats of the future,” Hegseth said, “will depend on funding the president’s vision for $1.5 trillion.”

entries.title: A Watchdog Group Is Challenging Jared Kushner’s Foreign Policy Role
entries.summary: The group’s lawsuit says the president’s son-in-law is a go-to foreign policy negotiator without Senate confirmation or financial disclosures.
entries.content:
An ethics watchdog organization filed a lawsuit Wednesday against Jared Kushner and the White House, seeking to bar the president's son-in-law from acting as a political envoy unless he’s confirmed by the Senate and files public financial disclosures.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington argues Kushner “holds a continuing position and wields significant government authority” while running an investment firm with over $6 billion under management, with about 99% owned by foreign investors.

“The interplay and overlap between his government role and private business interests present a heightened risk of financial conflicts of interest,” the lawsuit says. “Nonetheless, Kushner continues to exercise significant government power while circumventing the very protections put in place to guard against such conflicts.”

The organization is calling for the court to declare that Kushner is unlawfully working for the federal government and block White House Cabinet members and departments from supporting Kushner’s activities until he is confirmed by the Senate and files all financial disclosures.

In its complaint, CREW highlighted Kushner’s position as founder and CEO of Affinity Partners, a private investment firm based in Miami that is overwhelmingly backed by sovereign wealth funds in the Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

“The president’s son-in-law is currently acting with the authority of the United States government, shaping the most serious foreign policy and national security issues facing our nation, and yet, he has not complied with legal requirements to meaningfully assure the public of his competence and fitness, and that he’s putting America’s interests before his private interests,” said CREW President Donald K. Sherman in a press release.

The complaint also detailed Kushner’s growing involvement in President Donald Trump’s foreign negotiations since his first term, including his part as a major broker in negotiations in Israel, Russia and Ukraine in both official and informal capacities.

At the beginning of the year, Trump officially appointed Kushner as a ‘special envoy for peace’ and added him as an executive member of the inaugural Board of Peace.

In an email, Anna Kelly, the White House’s deputy press secretary, wrote that Kushner is a “proven dealmaker” with a record of success in assisting the president with foreign negotiations.

“CREW is an unserious, Trump-deranged organization that has been attacking President Trump, his family, and his administration since the first term,” Kelly wrote. “[Kushner’s] personal business activities have nothing to do with his diplomatic engagements, which he conducts on a volunteer basis at the President’s request and while paying his own expenses.”

Lawyers for CREW said Kushner continuing to work for the administration while evading the requirement for government authorities to file financial disclosures prevents the organization from accessing information that is “crucial to its work”.

“As long as Kushner occupies his diplomatic position without complying with these obligations, CREW will continue to be concretely harmed,” the lawsuit says.

The Constitution’s Appointments Clause and the Ethics in Government Act of 1978 require that individuals who hold continuing government positions be approved by the Senate before taking office and file public financial disclosures, respectively. Private citizens are prohibited from wielding government power.

entries.title: Trump Blames Biden for High Prices Hours After News of Rising Inflation
entries.summary: Despite voters’ affordability concerns, Trump tells crowd at Arizona rally the economy is hot and high oil costs are making the country “more money” than ever.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump told an Arizona crowd Wednesday that President Joe Biden is to blame for inflation, hours after the government reported that consumer prices had climbed again — with gas prices driving the increase.

“Whenever I have a news conference, somebody will stand up, say, ‘Mr. President, affordability,’” Trump said. “I said, ‘Yeah, that was caused by Biden, who gave us the highest inflation in history.’”

“The prices are all coming down,” Trump said while speaking at a campaign rally for Rep. Andy Biggs, the Republican gubernatorial nominee, in Bullhead City.

Affordability has been one of the defining issues in this year’s election cycle. The economy ranked as the top voting issue for 84% of registered voters — including 82% of those supporting Republicans, according to a Pew Research Center survey conducted Sept. 28-Oct. 4.

Gas prices continue to surge as a result of the Iran war, with the national average running over $1 per gallon more than it cost a year ago.

The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared to a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday. Prices rose 0.6% over the month, the largest monthly increase since April.

Gasoline prices rose 9.1% in September and accounted for more than half of the month’s consumer prices increase.

“I hated to do it, and I knew gasoline would go high, but I had no idea,” Trump said Wednesday of launching strikes on Iran earlier this year. “I thought it was going to go much higher.”

Trump has alternately promised relief and blamed his predecessor. But he again and again touted how well the economy is doing, at one point noting the stock market hitting “an all-time high.”

“Our country is making more money than it’s ever made because of the fact that oil is so high,” he said. “Because of the price of oil, Texas and Oklahoma and North Dakota and all these places, we’re making a fortune.”

Gas prices will fall precipitously once the war is over, Trump said, repeating a talking point he’s used often in recent months.

“Your gasoline is going to go down to even lower than it was before [the war] started,” Trump said.
