entries.title: Lawyers for New York Man Shot by ICE Agent Say Officer Fired Into His Car Without Warning
entries.summary: The account from Oscar Belgal's lawyers contrasts sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials.
entries.content:
By Philip Marcelo

NEW YORK (AP) — Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.

The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.”

The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal's release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.

“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way," Belgal's lawyers wrote. "Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”

New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn't conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.

The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.

A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.

Whatever happened next didn't appear on the NYPD's security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal's damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.

Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.

DHS didn't comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal's lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.

Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and is suffering from impaired hearing.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.

“Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, the lawyers representing Belgal.

At a news conference last week, Marcos Charles, the head of ICE's enforcement and removal operations, said Belgal refused orders to exit his vehicle and then accelerated and smashed into two government vehicles as ICE officers tried to block him from driving away.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has maintained officers didn’t know a child was in the car and blamed Belgal for putting his son's life in danger.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Voting Rights Groups Say Texas Failed to Process Voter Registrations
entries.summary: A lawsuit says counties “must now scramble to process this deluge of last-minute voter registrations ahead of the November 2026 election.”
entries.content:
Voting rights groups say Texas had failed to send almost 600,000 online voter registrations to county registrars as of last month, which could affect voters in the midterms.

In a lawsuit filed in Texas state court against the Texas Department of Public Safety and the Texas Secretary of State, the groups say counties “must now scramble to process this deluge of last-minute voter registrations ahead of the November 2026 election.”

The lawsuit also says that the hundreds of thousands of voters who are potentially affected “face the immediate injury of needing to take extra steps to vote because their voter registrations may not be updated before early voting for the 2026 general election.”

Early voting starts Oct. 19. DPS and the secretary of state’s office are legally required “to ensure that every eligible voter who submits a driver license application or renewal, or an update to his or her address with DPS not less than 30 days before an election, is registered to vote,” the lawsuit adds.

The lawsuit claims that the secretary of state’s “recent attempts to overhaul the statewide Texas Election Administration Management system” have caused delays. Vote Beat first reported on the lawsuit.

The voting rights groups — MOVE Texas Civic Fund and the Texas League of Women Voters — are arguing that the error violates a previous settlement agreement.

Texas has only guaranteed that voters can register online since that settlement was reached in 2021. The lawsuit claims that the inability for Texas residents to register or change their registration after moving within the state is a violation of the settlement agreement that promised them the right to register by mail in the first place.

And, the lawsuit alleges that these issues have been reported since mid-2025.

The groups included the declaration of Margaret Altizer, a Texas resident who moved in June to a different voting precinct. After trying to update her address and get a new voter registration in August, Altizer found herself still registered at her old address six weeks later.

Altizer said she is left with the option of casting a provisional ballot or voting in her old precinct, giving her no say in who represents her in the Texas state House.

Voting rights groups are asking the court to require the state properly perform its duties, maintain records of voter registrations and document errors to the court within the month.

Despite denials from the Texas DPS and the secretary of state’s office, the massive backlog was revealed in September, when counties suddenly received thousands of files at once.

“Harris County and Dallas County received approximately 75,000 and 68,000 late records from DPS respectively. Because of this deluge of applications, [Secretary of State] has offered counties grant funding to offset the additional costs of processing the files,” the lawsuit says.

That left counties scrambling to catch up before Nov. 3. The Texas secretary of state did not respond to a request for comment. The Texas DPS said they will not discuss pending litigation.
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's Phone Was Seized and Relatives Were Subpoenaed for Criminal Probe: AP Source
entries.summary: The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though DHS has suggested that authorities are examining her family’s immigration paperwork.
entries.content:
By Alanna Durkin Richer

Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker's phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.

The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar's immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar's Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.

The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.

On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on" related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker's financial disclosures.

“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.

The search of Omar's home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”

“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”

A phone message seeking comment was left Wednesday with a representative for Omar.

Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.

Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s 5th District, including Minneapolis. She is part of The Squad of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim-American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Trump Says Officials Who Leak Information to the Press ‘Should Be Shot’
entries.summary: The president has made several policy moves cracking down on press leaks, including sweeping NDAs for federal employees.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested that government officials who leak information to the media should be shot, referring to anyone who makes unauthorized disclosures to the press as “the scum of the earth.”

“In my opinion, leakers should be shot,” Trump said during an Arizona rally. “When they leak what time you're going to attack a country — and the reason you're attacking is really for defense because you don't want them to have a weapon that can blow up millions of people at one shot — now leakers should be dealt with very, very strongly.”

Minutes later, the president compared journalists to the leakers, saying members of the media are “almost as bad.”

“They leak false information that makes them a leaker,” Trump said, referencing members of the press. “Oftentimes without a source — I think they make up a lot of the sources.”

Since the start of his second term, Trump has directed several departments to impose strict rules on their staff to suppress unauthorized disclosures.

Last year, the Pentagon briefly instituted and proposed administering polygraphs to target alleged leakers.

For decades, government employees — particularly those working within the Department of Defense — have had to sign non-disclosure agreements covering classified information. But in May, the Trump administration proposed instituting a sweeping, government-wide NDAs for all federal employees.

The president also authorized the FBI to raid the home of Washington Post journalist Hannah Natanson in January, alleging her correspondence with a U.S. Navy veteran and Pentagon contractor, who had top-secret clearance but viewed and made copies of highly classified material without prior authorization, posed a national security threat. The Department of Justice arrested and charged Natanson’s source with the unauthorized retention and transmission of national defense information days before the raid on her home.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Supreme Court Sides With Republicans in Political Ad Price Fight
entries.summary: A lower court had given the FCC a 48-hour timeline to resolve a dispute over the agency’s policy on television ad rates for parties coordinating with candidates.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court once again sided with Republicans in a legal dispute over the price of political advertising — all but ensuring political parties will have access to low-cost rates when coordinating with candidates through the 2026 election.

In an unsigned decision, the court gave federal regulators more time to consider a challenge to party committees’ access to cheaper television and radio ads.

The Trump administration and Republican Party committees asked the Supreme Court last week to pause a ruling from the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that would have compelled the Federal Communications Commission to resolve a challenge by Democratic Senate nominees to guidelines issued by the agency in March.

To comply with the lower court order, “the FCC must triage its ongoing deliberation process and prepare its final order on an extremely expedited timeline,” the court wrote. Requiring the FCC to forego that process “is itself an injury that cannot be remedied after the fact,” the order says.

The new guidelines granted party committees’ access to lower television and radio ad rates when spending in coordination with candidates, who get lower ad rates in the runup to an election. The Supreme Court in June axed longstanding coordination limits between party committees and candidates, expanding party committees’ threshold for booking at lower rates.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson noted they would have denied Republicans' motion to stay the lower court decision.

The Trump administration and Republican Party committees argued at the Supreme Court that changing the rules so close to an election would cause too much uncertainty and urged the court to allow the FCC process to play out.

“Both orders irreparably injure political committees like the NRCC and NRSC by injecting uncertainty into their contracts, upsetting business deals, and ultimately depriving them of a statutory right on the eve of the election,” the party committees wrote in a filing Saturday in support of the stay. “The upcoming election demands consistency and predictability, not rushed changes.”

In a separate response, the Justice Department accused the Democratic Senate candidates of trying to “mute their opponents’ political speech.”

Shortly after the FCC issued the guidelines in March, Democratic candidates including Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia and former Sen. Sherrod Brown of Ohio challenged the agency's legal premise that party-coordinated ads qualify for the discounted rates.

In a separate ruling last month, the Supreme Court halted an appeals court ruling that would have outright blocked the political ad price guidelines.

Then, earlier this month, the appeals court accused the FCC of dragging its feet on the review and gave the agency 48 hours to resolve the legal dispute.

“The Commission cannot delay a decision until the eve of the election and then object to the clearly foreseeable consequences of that delay,” the candidates wrote in a response to the Supreme Court over the weekend.

The Supreme Court temporarily delayed the lower court’s deadline while it weighed the case, ultimately deciding it was “inappropriate.”

“The Communications Act requires the Commission to act on every application it receives, but it does not obligate the Commission to act within a particular timeframe,” the court wrote.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno

entries.title: A Judge Wants Hegseth to Answer for Transgender Troop Comments
entries.summary: Judge Ana Reyes said she expects the Defense Secretary to give straightforward answers about any “personal animus” — or face a deposition.
entries.content:
A federal judge gave Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth three weeks to answer 10 written questions about his personal feelings and thoughts about the U.S. military’s transgender ban.

At a court hearing Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes warned that she “has little patience” and expects the Defense Department’s top official to give straightforward answers that would shed light on any “personal animus.”

And Reyes said if she is not satisfied with Hegseth’s answers, she could force him into a one-hour deposition under oath.

The order came in a class-action lawsuit over the Trump administration’s hardline policy against transgender troops, and Hegseth’s answers could serve as evidence in an upcoming bench trial.

The lawsuit, filed last year, has challenged the U.S. military’s renewed prohibition against transgender service members, which followed two of President Donald Trump’s 2025 executive orders decrying “false ‘gender identity’” and “ideologues who deny the biological reality of sex.”

An Obama administration policy stopped the military from discharging people for being transgender in 2017. Trump reversed the policy in 2018, President Joe Biden undid that ban in 2021.

Hegseth’s attention-drawing comments are now threatening to play a central role in a lawsuit that argues the renewed ban is unconstitutional, arguing in part that it is based on animosity toward transgender people rather than the effectiveness of transgender service members.

In May 2025, Hegseth posted, “TRANS is out at the DOD.” At the Iowa State Fair in August, he used a slur when he said, “At the Department of War, we do training, not trannies.” Last week, Hegseth doubled down with a speech in which he said, “No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos.”

His statements came up in court in Washington, D.C., when government lawyers tried to block him from facing a deposition where he would be forced to answer questions from plaintiffs’ lawyers.

“I'm very aware that he is the secretary of defense and he has a lot of constraints on his time,” the judge said. “But he has time to tweet and put out videos and speak to generals, and I think it's fair game.”

Reyes also pointed out that Hegseth is claiming that “military readiness” would be compromised by soldiers who need gender-related medical care while simultaneously saying the U.S. government would begin testing soldiers for testosterone levels — and offer them testosterone replacement therapy to boost it.

“Secretary Hegseth issues a tweet. It was Secretary Hegseth who told his generals 'no trannies.' And I still haven’t mentioned that it was Secretary Hegseth that said individuals were going to get gender-affirming care ... while the policy says the military can't handle gender-affirming care,” Reyes said at the hearing.

After a back-and-forth with attorneys on both sides, the judge decided to take a two-step approach.

Class-action attorneys have a week to come up with 10 questions for Hegseth, and the defense secretary will then have three weeks to respond in writing. Reyes warned that she would not accept “very carefully tailored lawyerly responses that would say nothing.”

If that happens, Reyes said, she would be “happy to monitor the deposition.”

In 2025, Reyes temporarily enjoined the Trump policy in a ruling that concluded that the ban “is soaked in animus and dripping with pretext,” but the Supreme Court allowed the U.S. to implement it as the litigation played out.

In June, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit issued a split decision that paused the ban for those currently in the military but allowed it to remain in force for those wanting to join. The Trump administration in August appealed to the Supreme Court, which has not yet agreed to review the case.

entries.title: Confusion, Delays and Canceled Meetings: New Report Outlines a Chaotic Housing Department
entries.summary: A new study by the Government Accountability Office describes the confusion caused by staff reductions and other changes at HUD.
entries.content:
The Department of Housing and Urban Development reduced its workforce by 29% in 2025 as part of the White House’s broader effort to slash the size of the federal workforce, according to a new report released by the Government Accountability Office on Wednesday.

In total, 3,188 employees left the department from December 2024 to December 2025, largely through deferred resignation programs, according to the GAO. The report, which covered changes within the agency throughout fiscal year 2025, also said that more than half of the employees who left the department had worked at HUD for at least a decade, including many who had more than 20 years of service.

In the same period of time, nearly half of HUD’s grant programs did not award new grants due to new requirements set by the agency and delays on notices of funding opportunities, which organizations use to apply for federal dollars.

As a result of the staffing and funding changes, housing organizations that administer federally funded programs reported difficulties communicating with HUD and navigating its programs to the GAO. They reported canceled meetings, confusion and lapses in fair-housing grant funding.

“We interviewed 20 stakeholder organizations about these changes. Nearly all said that experienced points of contact had left,” the GAO report states. “Some stakeholders had to reduce services or staffing during funding gaps; others reported delays with physical inspections of properties.”

HUD did not respond to the GAO’s requests for information throughout the audit, according to the report. The study was based on interviews with stakeholders that included national housing organizations, federal grant recipients and public housing authorities, as well as an analysis of federal HUD data on spending and hiring.

The GAO also found that funding gaps and shifting guidance from HUD have made it harder to enforce fair-housing law — at the same time that the Trump administration has overhauled fair-housing enforcement and withdrawn guidance documents.

The study also found that only 32 of HUD’s 68 “active” grant programs made new awards in fiscal year 2025. HUD also terminated 144 federal contracts of 675 active contracts in that time, which resulted in spending being cut by approximately $367 million.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Massachusetts), the ranking member of the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee, and Rep. Maxine Waters (D-California), the ranking member of the House Financial Services Committee, along with other Democratic lawmakers, requested that the GAO conduct the audit.

The lawmakers admonished the Trump administration over its handling of the department. 

“This new report from the Congressional watchdog reveals that the Trump Administration is slashing housing program staff and illegally refusing to fund grants that help boost housing supply,” Warren said in a statement. “Trump’s draconian cuts mean that more Americans have fallen behind on rent, housing quality is getting worse, and enforcement against housing discrimination is all but eliminated.”

The White House and HUD did not respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

The report cites the Fair Housing Initiatives Program, which the federal government uses to fund organizations that conduct investigations of discrimination in housing, as one of the programs most affected by the administration’s actions.

One grantee told the GAO that their organization had “stopped all fair housing testing, accepted fewer new complaints, and referred potential clients elsewhere or to HUD” due to the lack of federal funding. Another said their organization had only opened 25 investigations since February 2025 after HUD terminated funding for its grants, “compared with 82 during the preceding 10 months” when their grant was active.
